Anxiety showed little evidence of consistent benefit. Additional outcomes, including sleep, cortisol, heart rate, and pain, were sparse but generally directionally favorable. Most studies had high, serious, or critical risk of bias.

Conclusion

The available evidence does not establish that CWE improves mood, depressive symptoms, perceived stress, wellbeing, or related outcomes. The evidence remains limited, heterogeneous, and at substantial risk of bias, and several estimates became smaller in controlled only analyses. CWE should not currently be regarded as a standalone treatment for psychiatric disorders. Larger controlled trials are needed to clarify clinical relevance, safety, mechanisms, and optimal use.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420250654531.

records.title: Artificial intelligence in membranous nephropathy: transforming clinical management toward precision medicine.

content.title: Artificial intelligence in membranous nephropathy: transforming clinical management toward precision medicine.
content.abstract: Membranous Nephropathy (MN) is the leading cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults, characterized by significant clinical heterogeneity ranging from spontaneous remission to end-stage kidney disease. Current management of membranous nephropathy, which relies heavily on renal biopsy and static serological markers such as anti-PLA2R antibodies, often fails to predict individual disease trajectories. This limitation frequently leads to empirical immunosuppressive therapy with a trial-and-error approach. This review explores the transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in reshaping MN management from evidence-based to data-driven and predictive medicine. We examine AI-driven innovations across the clinical spectrum: from computational pathology systems that automate glomerular morphometry with high objectivity and reproducibility, to non-invasive diagnostic models integrating radiomics and serology for non-invasive diagnosis. In therapeutics, we discuss machine learning algorithms that predict individual responses to Rituximab versus Cyclophosphamide, enabling personalized regimen selection. Furthermore, we highlight the role of AI in prognostic stratification, where dynamic in silico patient models and multi-omics integration unravel molecular subtypes and forecast renal survival with high granularity. While acknowledging critical challenges such as data silos, model interpretability gaps, and the need for global validation, we conclude that AI serves as a powerful augmentation tool. By synthesizing high-dimensional data into actionable insights, AI has the potential to facilitate increasingly predictive, preventative, and personalized care strategies in MN management.

records.title: Controversies and consensus on immune function and long-term health risks following adult thymectomy: a comprehensive review of molecular mechanisms and real-world evidence.

content.title: Controversies and consensus on immune function and long-term health risks following adult thymectomy: a comprehensive review of molecular mechanisms and real-world evidence.
content.abstract:
Objective

To evaluate the long-term immunological, oncological, and clinical consequences of adult thymectomy by synthesizing recent basic, translational, and real-world clinical evidence.

Background

Historical surgical paradigms regarded the post-pubertal adult thymus as an immunologically redundant, fatty involuted organ, justifying routine "incidental" resection during cardiac procedures. A high-profile 2023 cohort study in The New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) challenged this concept, reporting that adult thymectomy significantly increased 5-year all-cause mortality and cancer risk. Subsequent population-level studies (US SEER/NCDB, French PMSI) and deep-learning imaging cohorts have sparked debate, offering both corroborating and conflicting insights into adult thymic function.

Methods and synthesis

This review synthesizes cellular mechanisms (TREC dynamics, TCR repertoire contraction, senescence-associated T cells, Treg lineage stability) and endocrine factors (thymulin-mediated myeloid regulation) with clinical data stratified by age at surgery, indication, resection extent, and follow-up duration.

Conclusions

The adult thymus remains functionally active, exporting naïve T cells and humoral immunomodulators like thymulin that maintain peripheral immune tolerance and restrain inflammaging. Clinical evaluation must differentiate between incidental resection (which induces avoidable iatrogenic immunosenescence) and therapeutic resection (e.g., for thymic epithelial tumors or myasthenia gravis), where removing a diseased, immunosuppressive microenvironment can reduce secondary cancer risk. Partial thymectomy (PT) is emerging as an option to preserve immunocompetence when oncologically feasible.

records.title: Opportunities and Challenges of Using Artificial Intelligence in Predicting Clinical Outcomes and Length of Stay in Neonatal Intensive Care Units: Systematic Review.

content.title: Opportunities and Challenges of Using Artificial Intelligence in Predicting Clinical Outcomes and Length of Stay in Neonatal Intensive Care Units: Systematic Review.
content.abstract:
Background

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in health care has been steadily increasing for over 2 decades. Integrating AI into neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) has promise as it has the potential to reshape neonatal care and improve outcomes. However, challenges such as data quality, clinical interpretation, and ethical considerations may hinder AI's practical implementation in NICUs.

Objective

This study aims (1) to analyze the current AI research landscape for predicting clinical outcomes and length of stay in the NICU and (2) to explore the benefits and challenges of using AI in the NICU for these predictions.

Methods

A systematic review was conducted across 6 databases-PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, Informit, and La Trobe Library-to identify English-language peer-reviewed articles published between January 2017 and March 2023 that focused on the use of AI for predicting length of stay and clinical outcomes for NICU patients. Eligibility criteria excluded studies outside the NICU context or lacking predictive focus. Both prospective and retrospective designs were included. A thematic analysis of AI applications in NICUs from the articles identified was conducted.

Results

A total of 24 studies were included in the review, comprising 15 retrospective and 9 prospective designs. These studies primarily originated from the United States (13 studies), with others from Austria, Taiwan, and other countries. The studies evaluated AI applications in NICU settings to predict comorbidities (18/24), mortality (4/24), and length of stay (2/24). Sixteen studies were in the exploration stage, lacking cohesive AI strategies, while 8 demonstrated systematic exploration but no fully integrated solutions. The synthesis of results identified key applications of AI in NICU care, including data-driven insights and predictive models, advancements in medical imaging, improved risk stratification, and personalized neonatal care. AI showed promise in enhancing diagnostic accuracy and care planning, but significant challenges persist, such as data quality, model generalization, and ethical concerns. No studies reported a fully integrated AI ecosystem, highlighting the need for further research to bridge gaps and realize AI's transformative potential in neonatal care.

Conclusions

This review highlights the potential of AI in improving NICU care, particularly through predictive models, medical imaging, and personalized interventions. However, the evidence is limited by significant methodological variability, small sample sizes, risk of bias, and a lack of external validation in included studies. Many studies remain in exploratory phases without cohesive AI strategies or integration into clinical practice, limiting the practical applicability of findings. These results underscore the importance of addressing challenges such as data quality, model generalization, and ethical considerations to fully realize AI's potential in neonatal care. Future research should focus on robust validation, comprehensive implementation strategies, and ethical frameworks to ensure AI's effective and responsible integration into NICU settings.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Pathology for Preoperative Lymphovascular Invasion and Metastatic Risk Prediction in Breast Cancer: Bridging the Biopsy-Resection Gap.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Pathology for Preoperative Lymphovascular Invasion and Metastatic Risk Prediction in Breast Cancer: Bridging the Biopsy-Resection Gap.
content.abstract: Breast cancer is a leading global diagnosis where lymphovascular invasion (LVI) serves as a critical indicator of metastatic potential. Conventional assessment is often hindered by its reliance on postoperative findings, sampling errors, and subjective interobserver variability. This review evaluates how artificial intelligence (AI), digital pathology, and MRI radiomics provide earlier, quantitative estimations of LVI-related risk. The strongest direct evidence currently comes from MRI-based studies, where validation performance often reaches area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.84-0.90. By contrast, digital pathology is especially mature for LVI-adjacent tasks such as lymph node metastasis detection and slide-based relapse-risk modelling, which together provide an important translational foundation for future LVI-specific tools. This review also addresses issues that remain underdeveloped in the literature, including the distinction between lymphatic and vascular invasion, AI-specific risk-of-bias and reporting frameworks, the emerging regulatory landscape for adjacent breast AI tools, and the gap between resection-based development datasets and biopsy-level preoperative use. Although most modern computational models are developed using extensive surgical resection specimens, their true clinical utility hinges on successful validation and performance within the highly restricted, fragmented tissue context of preoperative core needle biopsies. Overall, the field appears most promising when LVI prediction is framed not as an isolated binary task, but as one component of a broader metastatic-risk workflow that supports calibrated, multidisciplinary breast cancer decision-making.

records.title: Reimagining nursing practice in the era of AI: a qualitative systematic review and meta-synthesis of nurses' lived experiences.
records.publisher: Journal of health, population, and nutrition

content.title: Reimagining nursing practice in the era of AI: a qualitative systematic review and meta-synthesis of nurses' lived experiences.
content.abstract:
Introduction

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare is transforming nursing practice, introducing both opportunities and challenges. This qualitative systematic review and meta-synthesis examines nurses' encounters with AI technologies across clinical, managerial, and educational domains. It aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of nurses' lived experiences with AI technologies across clinical, managerial, and educational domains, identify barriers and facilitators to its integration, and derive an interpretive framework for nurses' positioning in AI-enhanced care environments.

Methods

Following PRISMA and ENTREQ guidelines, a comprehensive literature search was conducted across PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase for peer-reviewed qualitative studies from January 2017 to June 2025. The SPIDER framework defined eligibility, focusing on nurses' experiences with AI. Two reviewers independently screened 284 deduplicated records, with 26 studies included after full-text review. Data were extracted using a tailored form, and quality was assessed via the CASP checklist. A combined meta-ethnography and thematic analysis synthesized findings, generating themes through iterative coding and consensus. Verbatim quotes ensured fidelity to nurses' voices, with methodological rigor maintained through reflexivity and member checking.

Results

Five themes emerged from 26 studies: (1) Enhancing Clinical Efficiency and Decision-Making, where AI improves risk prediction and workflows; (2) Navigating Barriers to AI Integration, highlighting technical and organizational challenges; (3) Ethical and Cultural Considerations, emphasizing patient autonomy and bias concerns; (4) Evolving Nursing Roles, reflecting shifts to supervisory and technical competencies; and (5) AI's Role in Enhancing Communication, noting its facilitation and depersonalization risks. Nurses value AI's efficiency but stress user-friendly design and ethical safeguards. Continuous training is needed to balance technical skills with empathy.

Conclusion

AI significantly enhances nursing efficiency and decision-making but introduces technical, ethical, and role-related challenges. User-centered AI design, comprehensive training, and ethical frameworks are essential to address barriers and biases. Nurses' evolving roles require balancing technical proficiency with humanistic care. Future research should explore longitudinal impacts to ensure AI supports equitable, patient-centered nursing practice.

records.title: The effects of physical exercise on executive function, internalizing symptoms and externalizing symptoms in children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: The effects of physical exercise on executive function, internalizing symptoms and externalizing symptoms in children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

The aim of this study is to comprehensively assess the potential effects of physical exercise on executive function, internalizing symptoms and externalizing symptoms in children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and to explore the moderating factors influencing these effects.

Methods

We performed a systematic search of six databases (including Web of Science, PubMed, Embase, PsycNET, the Cochrane Library and SPORTDiscus). Data analysis was performed using R software, and a meta-analysis was conducted using a random-effects model to estimate the pooled effect size. In addition, subgroup analyses and meta-regression were conducted to explore potential moderating factors.

Results

A total of 25 randomised controlled trials involving 1,116 participants were included. With low certainty of evidence, the pooled effect of inhibitory control was statistically significant (g = 0.45, p < 0.01). With very low certainty of evidence, the pooled effect of internalizing symptoms was statistically significant (g = 0.97, p = 0.03). The pooled effects of cognitive flexibility (g = 0.69, p = 0.054), working memory (g = 0.28, p = 0.10), and externalizing symptoms (g = 0.64, p = 0.29) did not reach statistical significance, all rated as very low certainty of evidence.

Conclusion

Physical exercise may be positively associated with inhibitory control in children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, the effects of interventions show high heterogeneity, have wide confidence intervals, and exhibit limited stability.

Systematic review registration

PROSPERO CRD420261380631.

records.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Radiological Diagnosis of Urogynecological and Obstetric Disorders: A Narrative Review.

content.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Radiological Diagnosis of Urogynecological and Obstetric Disorders: A Narrative Review.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative tool in radiological diagnosis, particularly in urogynaecology and obstetric disorders where accurate and timely imaging is essential. This narrative review evaluates current AI applications across key imaging modalities, including ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging, emphasizing improvements in diagnostic precision, automation, and workflow efficiency. AI-driven approaches such as machine learning, deep learning, and radiomics enable automated segmentation, anomaly detection, and quantitative assessment of conditions, including pelvic floor dysfunction, urinary incontinence, endometriosis, and fetal abnormalities. In obstetric imaging, AI supports automated fetal biometry, anomaly detection, and risk prediction for complications such as preeclampsia and preterm birth. Integration of AI into radiological workflows enhances reporting efficiency and facilitates clinical decision-making through predictive analytics and standardized outputs. Challenges related to data quality, model generalizability, interpretability, and regulatory frameworks continue to limit widespread clinical adoption. Future directions should focus on multicenter datasets, explainable AI, and multimodal integration to improve reliability and clinical translation. Furthermore, strengthening clinician-AI collaboration and incorporating real-world validation studies will be critical for safe implementation. Overall, AI has significant potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy, reduce variability, and support personalized care in women's imaging.

records.title: Dumbbell Bench Press and Dumbbell Fly Elicit Similar Pectoralis Major Muscle Hypertrophy in Recreationally Trained Men.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Dumbbell Bench Press and Dumbbell Fly Elicit Similar Pectoralis Major Muscle Hypertrophy in Recreationally Trained Men.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Dell'Avanzi, FG, Enes, A, Alves-Marques, F, Costa-Rodrigues, J, Bello, G, Seima, G, Nass, G, Moreira, NF, Santana, C, Mohan, AE, Piñero, A, Schoenfeld, BJ, and Souza-Junior, TP. Dumbbell bench press and dumbbell fly elicit similar pectoralis major muscle hypertrophy in recreationally trained men. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Exercise selection is one of the main resistance training (RT) variables for eliciting inhomogeneous muscle growth. Whether exercises that differ in resistance moment arm elicit whole- and nonuniform hypertrophy of the pectoralis major remains unclear. This study investigated the effects of the dumbbell bench press (DBP) and dumbbell fly (DFLY) on pectoralis major muscle thickness (MT). Twenty-six young healthy men (RT experience 3.3 ± 3.1 years) were allocated to DBP or DFLY groups, training twice a week over a 10-week period. The weekly set number was individualized according to subjects' previous RT pectoralis major volume. Pectoralis major MT was assessed by ultrasound imaging at medial (30%), intermediate (50%), and lateral (70%) sites at baseline and postintervention. Our mixed-model analysis indicated a main effect for time (p < 0.05) but no time-by-group interaction for the medial site (p = 0.500), intermediate site (p = 0.864), lateral site (p = 0.720), and the sum of the MT across sites (p = 0.985). Therefore, both exercises elicited similar general and regional hypertrophy on pectoralis major MT in recreationally trained individuals. Coaches and practitioners can select DBP or DFLY when targeting pectoralis major muscle development in recreationally trained men based on personal preference and goals within the RT program.

records.title: Is plant-based protein supplementation as effective as whey protein? A systematic review and meta-analysis in untrained adults undergoing resistance training.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Is plant-based protein supplementation as effective as whey protein? A systematic review and meta-analysis in untrained adults undergoing resistance training.
content.abstract:
Background

Dietary protein supplements are commonly consumed to support increases in lean body mass among healthy adults engaged in resistance training (RT). Although whey protein has been extensively investigated, plant-based protein supplements have emerged as a viable alternative for individuals who avoid animal-derived products.

Methods

The present study aims to evaluate, through a systematic review and meta-analysis, the effects of plant-based versus whey protein supplementation on body composition in untrained adults (18-59 years) undergoing RT, using Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DEXA). The systematic review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 checklist and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251145410). Searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect, identifying 5 studies that met the inclusion criteria for qualitative synthesis and meta-analysis.

Results

When combined with RT, both plant-based and whey protein supplementation were associated with improvements in lean body mass (LBM) and body fat mass (BFM), with no significant between-group differences observed.

Conclusions

Thus, soy- and pea-based protein supplements may support favorable body composition changes in adults initiating RT and could be considered practical nutritional options for individuals seeking alternatives to whey protein. Regarding chia-based protein, the available evidence is currently limited to a single study that did not demonstrate significant changes in lean body mass; therefore, firm conclusions regarding its efficacy cannot be drawn at this time.

records.title: How Often Should Volume Increase? Effects of Different Volume-Progression Frequencies on Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Women.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: How Often Should Volume Increase? Effects of Different Volume-Progression Frequencies on Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Women.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Enes, A, Macedo, ACG, Nass, G, Costa-Rodrigues, J, Alves-Marques, F, Santana, C, Dell'Avanzi, FG, Rodrigues, BG, Alves, RC, De Souza, EO, and Souza-Junior, TP. How often should volume increase? Effects of different volume-progression frequencies on strength and hypertrophy adaptations in females. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Resistance training (RT) volume is an important programming variable for strength and hypertrophy. However, how frequently RT volume should be progressed remains unclear. Thus, we investigated the effects of progressively increasing RT volume by 2 weekly sets targeting the quadriceps femoris every 2 weeks (2 W) or every 4 weeks (4 W) over a 12-week period in recreationally trained women. Using a within-subject design and accounting for previous RT volume, 21 subjects (age 23.3 ± 3.9 years; RT experience 1.1 ± 0.7 years) had their limbs assigned to one of the 2 conditions: 2 weeks (2 W) or 4 weeks (4 W). 45° leg-press 1-repetition maximum (1RM) and the sum of muscle thickness (∑MT) of the proximal (30%), middle (50%), and distal (70%) portions of the lateral thigh were assessed at baseline and after 12 weeks. Our mixed-model analysis indicated a main effect of time for 1RM (p < 0.0001), with no difference between the 2 and 4 W conditions (p = 0.317). Similarly, regarding the ∑MT, the analysis indicated a main effect of time (p < 0.001), with no difference between the conditions (p = 0.616). Within the relatively high training volumes examined, progressing the RT volume by 2 weekly sets every 2 or 4 weeks did not elicit detectable differences in strength and hypertrophy adaptations over 12 weeks in recreationally trained women.

records.title: Lower-Body Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Response to Concurrent Training in Trained Young Males.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Lower-Body Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Response to Concurrent Training in Trained Young Males.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Gomes, M, Costa, M, Pezarat-Correia, P, and Mendonca, GV. Lower-body strength and hypertrophy adaptations in response to concurrent training in trained young males. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study examined the interference effect of concurrent training (CT) on maximal and explosive strength and muscle morphology in trained young males. Thirty subjects were randomly assigned to endurance training (E), resistance training (R), or CT for 11 weeks. The intervention comprised 2 mesocycles: weeks 1-5 emphasizing maximal strength, and weeks 6-11 targeting explosive strength. Assessments were conducted at baseline, mid-training, and post-training, and included leg-press maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC), rate of force development (RFD), countermovement jump kinetics, and vastus lateralis cross-sectional area and pennation angle. Maximal voluntary isometric contraction increased only in the R group (18.4 ± 10.2%, p = 0.015). Peak RFD improved in both R (31.8 ± 23.2%) and CT (23.1 ± 27.9%), although with distinct time courses: R improved progressively across both mesocycles, whereas CT improved only during the second. Early-phase RFD (0-50 ms) increased in the R group from mid-training onward, whereas the CT group improved only from mid- to post-training (38.3 ± 40.4%, p = 0.021), accompanied by greater quadriceps electromyographic activity (p < 0.05). No changes in RFD were observed in E during training. Countermovement jump positive impulse improved in both R (12.7 ± 9.0%) and CT (8.8 ± 8.3%, p < 0.05), with no evidence of interference in jump-related explosive performance. Cross-sectional area increased in both R (17.0 ± 13.0%) and CT (8.8 ± 9.4%, p < 0.05). Pennation angle increased in CT (10.1 ± 12.9%) and R (18.6 ± 15.1%). These findings indicate that, although CT may limit MVIC development and delay early-phase RFD adaptations, it does not hinder explosive performance when resistance training is oriented toward rapid-strength development. Thus, CT can be effectively implemented in trained individuals when resistance training is periodized to emphasize neural-driven explosive or hypertrophy-related adaptations.

records.title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Chilingirian-Padrón, R, Álvarez-Yates, T, and García-García, O. Effects of in-season contrast strength training on jump performance and sprint ability in female field hockey players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 6-week in-season contrast strength training program incorporating sport-specific tasks on neuromuscular performance in sub-elite female field hockey players. Twenty-five athletes completed a pre-post single-cohort intervention integrated into their regular team schedule. Each session consisted of 3 sequential blocks: (a) a high-load strength exercise targeting maximal strength or hypertrophy (70-85% 1 repetition maximum [1RM]); (b) a biomechanically related explosive action performed at low load (∼30% 1RM) and high execution velocity; and (c) a high-speed sport-specific task. Jump performance was assessed using bilateral and unilateral countermovement jumps (CMJs) and free arm CMJ, whereas sprint ability was evaluated through 10- and 20-m sprints. A mixed-model repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to determine the effects of the intervention, with Time (Pre, Post) as within-subject factor and Playing Position (defenders, midfielders, forwards) as between-subject factor, with the level of significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements were observed in all jump and sprint assessments: jump performance increased by 5.7-29.6%, whereas sprint ability improved by 1.6-1.9%. These findings indicate that 6 weeks of contrast strength training incorporating high-speed sports-specific tasks performed during the competitive season elicited meaningful improvements in stretch-shortening cycle-related jump performance and sprint ability in sub-elite female field hockey players.

records.title: Comparative Effects of Resistance Training and High-Intensity Interval Training on Body Composition, Metabolic Health, and Functional Strength in Overweight and Obese Adults: A 12-Week Randomized Controlled Trial.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Comparative Effects of Resistance Training and High-Intensity Interval Training on Body Composition, Metabolic Health, and Functional Strength in Overweight and Obese Adults: A 12-Week Randomized Controlled Trial.
content.abstract: Petisco-Rodríguez, C, Barroso-Hernández, Á, Bartolomé-Sánchez, I, and Crego, A. Comparative effects of resistance training and high-intensity interval training on body composition, metabolic health, and functional strength in overweight and obese adults: A 12-week randomized controlled trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to compare the effects of 2 training programs on anthropometric and physiological variables in overweight and obese adults. Ninety subjects (age = 39.9 ± 10.4 years; body mass index (BMI) = 31.0 ± 4.3 kg·m-2) were randomly assigned to a resistance training group (RG; n = 30), a high-intensity interval training (HIIT) group (HG; n = 30), or a nontraining control group (CG; n = 30). Both the RG and HG performed 2 weekly sessions for 12 weeks. The RG completed 8 upper-body and lower-body resistance exercises at 70% of 1 repetition maximum, while the HG performed high-intensity intervals at 80% of the maximum heart rate. A 3 (group: CG, RG, HG) × 2 (time: pre, post) mixed ANOVA revealed significant effects on the BMI, body fat, and fasting glucose. Both training groups showed similar improvements in all measures from preintervention to postintervention. Compared with CG, RG and HG had reduced body fat and BMI, while RG demonstrated greater gains in muscle mass, fasting glucose, and grip strength. Paired t-tests confirmed significant within-group improvements in BMI, body fat, grip strength, and fasting glucose in the RG and HG. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.017 after the Bonferroni correction. These findings suggest that both resistance training and HIIT enhance the body composition of overweight and obese adults. However, resistance training may provide additional benefits in muscular fitness and glycemic control, supporting its role as a practical strategy for improving metabolic health in this population.

records.title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women Soccer Players and Its Relationship With Quality of Life and Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women Soccer Players and Its Relationship With Quality of Life and Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Sebastian-Rico, JM, Muñoz-Fernández, MJ, Martínez-Aranda, LM, Calvo-Lluch, Á, and Ortega-Becerra, M. Effectiveness of pelvic floor muscle training in women soccer players and its relationship with quality of life and pelvic floor muscle strength: a randomized controlled pilot study. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study investigated the effects of a 6-week pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) program on muscle strength, function, and the prevalence of related dysfunctions in professional female soccer players using a randomized controlled pilot study design. Twenty nulliparous professional soccer players from the Spanish professional league (2024-2025 season) were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n = 12) or a control group (n = 8). Assessments included anthropometric data, validated questionnaires (International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire-Short Form and Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), clinical interviews, and physical examination using the PERFECT method and manometry. The intervention consisted of a 6-week supervised PFMT program (4 sessions/week, 30 minutes each) progressed through 4 phases: education, proprioception, strengthening, and functional integration. Results showed significant group × time interactions for pelvic floor self-efficacy (Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), with scores in the PFMT group increasing by 48.8 and 59.6% (p < 0.05), representing large between-group effect sizes (d = 0.91-1.26). Pelvic floor muscle performance increased by 122.4% in the intervention group (d = 1.25), whereas no meaningful changes were observed in the control group. No adverse events were reported. In conclusion, a 6-week supervised PFMT program is an effective and safe intervention for professional female soccer players, significantly improving muscle function and self-efficacy. These findings support the integration of PFMT for both therapeutic and preventive purposes in elite, high-impact sports environments.

records.title: Lower-limb performance and muscle soreness after short-term dark chocolate intake in CrossFit®-trained women: an exploratory secondary analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Lower-limb performance and muscle soreness after short-term dark chocolate intake in CrossFit®-trained women: an exploratory secondary analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Dark chocolate (DC) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for exercise performance and recovery, but evidence in trained women remains limited. This exploratory secondary analysis examined selected lower-limb performance outcomes and delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) in female CrossFit® athletes.

Methods

This secondary analysis included 15 trained female CrossFit® athletes from a randomized crossover trial. No separate a priori sample-size calculation was performed for these outcomes (minimum detectable paired effect, d_z = 0.78). DC (30 g/day, 85% cocoa), placebo chocolate (PLA), and an open-label control (CONN) were compared at four operationally defined menstrual-cycle assessments after three days of supplementation. DC-PLA allocation was blinded, but blinding success was not assessed. Outcomes were vertical jump height (VJH), knee isokinetic and isometric performance, and muscle-specific DOMS after the Cindy WOD.

Results

Condition effects survived FDR control for VJH and 19 of 22 dynamometry outcomes. Across assessments, VJH was 34.48 ± 5.09 cm with DC and 30.22 ± 2.34 cm with PLA (mean difference 4.27 cm, 95% CI 1.45 to 7.08; Holm-adjusted p = 0.017; g_av = 1.09). No condition-by-assessment interaction survived FDR control (all q ≥ 0.141). DOMS showed significant time effects for all three muscles, peaked at approximately 24 h, remained elevated at 48 h, and declined toward baseline by 72 h. A condition-by-time effect remained significant only for gastrocnemius soreness (Holm-adjusted p = 0.012; ηp2 = 0.212); no DOMS condition main effect or condition-by-assessment-by-time interaction was supported.

Conclusion

DC was associated with higher values for selected lower-limb outcomes, but these exploratory findings do not establish phase-specific efficacy, equivalent effects across cycle assessments, or a consistent DOMS benefit. Unusually large performance estimates and unmodeled period and carryover effects warrant caution.

records.title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Campos, BT, Rodrigues, JGdS, Cal Abad, CC, Bachi, ALL, dos Santos, CMM, Tritto, AC, Kons, RL, Penna, EM, and Prado, LS. Performance and physiological responses to strength training programs in elite judo athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study compared the effects of 2 short-term strength training models, block planning (BP) and undulating planning (UP), on performance, physiological, and perceptual responses in elite judo athletes. We hypothesized that BP would induce greater physiological strain due to the concentration of training stimuli. Eighteen judokas (14 men and 4 women) were randomly assigned to BP (n = 9) or UP (n = 9) for 4 weeks, performing 6 weekly strength sessions alongside technical-tactical training. Performance outcomes included countermovement jump (CMJ), muscle power (back squat and bent-over row), and the Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT). Monitoring variables included internal load, heart rate variability (HRV), and well-being, while physiological markers included creatine kinase, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and cortisol. Data were analyzed using 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (p < 0.05). Both groups improved SJFT performance (p < 0.01), with no between-group differences. Block planning increased lower-limb peak power (p = 0.01; d = 0.90), whereas UP showed no meaningful change. Upper-limb power and CMJ did not change in either group. Internal load showed different temporal patterns between models. Block planning presented higher HRVcv values (p = 0.04), indicating greater autonomic perturbation. Creatine kinase and TNF-α increased over time in both groups (p ≤ 0.05), while cortisol showed an interaction without clear post hoc differences. In conclusion, BP improved lower-limb power but increased physiological strain, whereas UP elicited similar judo-specific improvements with lower recovery demands. These findings highlight the importance of training organization for balancing performance and recovery in elite judo athletes.

records.title: The effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition and influence of FTO genotype in exercise-trained men and women.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: The effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition and influence of FTO genotype in exercise-trained men and women.
content.abstract:
Background

High-protein diets have consistently been associated with favorable changes in body composition in both sedentary and exercise-trained populations. Despite abundant evidence supporting protein intakes above the recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for active individuals, the effects of deliberate protein overfeeding, particularly in those already consuming adequate protein, remain incompletely characterized. The primary purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition in exercise-trained men and women. The secondary purpose was to determine whether body composition adaptations differed by FTO rs9939609 genotype.

Methods

Fifty-six exercise-trained men and women (age: 22.40 ± 5.78 years; body mass: 75.47 ± 14.98 kg; BMI: 24.52 ± 3.50 kg/m2; resistance training: 5.12 ± 3.35 h/week) were enrolled in a 4-week dietary intervention. Participants were instructed to increase their daily protein intake by approximately 20% above baseline while maintaining habitual training. Body composition was assessed pre- and post-intervention using a multi-frequency bioelectrical impedance device (InBody® 270). Dietary intake was self-monitored via MyFitnessPal®. Thirty-five participants completed both pre- and post-testing assessments and constituted the primary analysis. Linear regression models adjusted for baseline values indicated that FTO genotype was not a significant predictor of body composition changes (p > 0.05).

Results

Protein intake trended toward a significant increase over the 4-week period (pre: 146 ± 66 g/day vs. post: 164 ± 79 g/day; p = 0.053), representing an approximate 12% increase. Total energy intake, carbohydrate, and fat intake did not significantly change. Lean body mass increased significantly (pre: 59.95 ± 14.14 kg vs. post: 60.62 ± 14.42 kg; p = 0.005; Cohen's d = 0.31) and total body water increased significantly (pre: 43.85 ± 10.35 L vs. post: 44.34 ± 10.55 L; p = 0.005). Fat mass (p = 0.424), body fat percentage (p = 0.149), and total body mass (p = 0.09) did not significantly change.

Conclusions

A 4-week modest protein overfeeding protocol in exercise-trained men and women was associated with a significant increase in lean body mass and total body water without concomitant increases in fat mass. These adaptations were not modified by FTO rs9939609 genotype. These findings support the contention that higher protein intakes do not promote fat accretion and may facilitate improvements in body composition in trained individuals.

records.title: Do Putative Human Reticulospinal Tract Properties Adapt Following Short-Term Isometric Resistance Training?
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Do Putative Human Reticulospinal Tract Properties Adapt Following Short-Term Isometric Resistance Training?
content.abstract:
Purpose

The primary purpose of this study was to investigate whether isometric resistance training (RT) leads to reticulospinal tract (RST) adaptations.

Methods

A "RT group" of 30 healthy adults completed 4 weeks (15 sessions) of volume-matched unilateral elbow flexion RT involving high (32 repetitions/session at 70% maximal voluntary torque [MVT]) or low (64 repetitions/session at 35%MVT) loads. An additional 15 participants served as controls (CON group). Pre- and post-test MVT, RST properties (RST gain ratio derived from the StartReact assessment; startling auditory stimulus-conditioned/control motor evoked potential [MEP] ratio; and startling stimulus-conditioned/control cervicomedullary MEP [CMEP] ratio), CST excitability and intracortical inhibition properties (in response to transcranial magnetic stimulation) were assessed.

Results

MVT increased more in the RT group (+12.8%; n = 30) vs. CON group (-4.3%; n = 15; group (2) × time (2), p = 0.001). However, changes in RST properties assessed using a series of indirect measures did not differ between the RT group (-1.4% to 6.6%; n = 30) and CON group (-4.5% to 10.5%; n = 15; group (2) × time (2), 0.352 ≤ p ≤ 0.834).

Conclusions

RST adaptations within a sample of healthy young men and women, assessed using various indirect measurement approaches, did not occur following only 4 weeks of isometric elbow flexion RT. These findings add to the currently limited scientific evidence from short-term human RT intervention studies available to inform the use of RT for healthy individuals or patients primarily targeting the development of RST function.

records.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
content.abstract:
Purpose

The present study aimed to evaluate associations between resistance training and binge drinking in relation to musculoskeletal composition, physical fitness, cognitive function, and psychological wellness in young adult females.

Methods

Participants were categorized into four groups: sedentary low alcohol consumers (SL; n=12), sedentary binge drinkers (SB; n=12), resistance-trained low alcohol consumers (RTL; n=12), and resistance-trained binge drinkers (RTB; n=12). Measurements included body composition via DEXA scan, muscle quality via ultrasonography, and insulin sensitivity via oral glucose tolerance test. Physical performance was assessed using maximum chair stand power, vertical jump, broad jump, knee extensor torque, grip strength, and push-ups to failure. Tests and questionnaires were used to assess cognitive function and psychological wellness.

Results

Resistance-trained females had lower body fat than sedentary females (RTL = 29.28±4.27%; RTB = 29.03±3.67%; SL = 37.18±5.32%; SB = 34.83±3.54%; p<0.05), and RTL had more fat-free mass than SL and SB (RTL = 48.31±5.81 kg; SL = 38.08±6.59 kg; SB = 40.37±6.05 kg; both p<0.05). There were no differences between RTL and RTB in bone mineral density, muscle quality, or physical performance. RTL outperformed SL and SB on vertical jump (both p<0.05) while RTB outperformed SL and SB on broad jump. RTL had lower fasting blood glucose than RTB (88.92±12.09 mg/dL and 103.17 ± 10.21 mg/dL, respectively; p=0.008), and lower postprandial blood glucose than all groups (RTL = 103.83±19.82 mg/dL; RTB = 137.58±21.54 mg/dL; SL = 148.50±44.60 mg/dL; SB = 139.25±14.49 mg/dL; all p<0.05).

Conclusions

The results suggest that ≥1 year of binge drinking is associated with poorer metabolic health without differences in performance in young females. Further, frequent RT may mitigate the effects of binge drinking on body composition.

records.title: Exploratory serum renal biomarker and eGFR responses to high-protein diets during resistance versus concurrent training in resistance-trained men.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Exploratory serum renal biomarker and eGFR responses to high-protein diets during resistance versus concurrent training in resistance-trained men.
content.abstract:
Background

High protein intake is common among resistance-trained athletes, but its association with renal biomarkers across different exercise modalities remains uncertain. This study investigated whether consuming a high-protein diet (3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹) during 16 weeks of resistance training (RT) or concurrent training (CT) affects renal biomarkers and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in resistance-trained men.

Methods

Forty-eight resistance-trained men (26 ± 6 years; BMI 25.6 ± 2.9 kg·m⁻²) were randomized to 16 weeks of RT or CT (4 sessions·wk⁻¹) while consuming either 1.6 or 3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ of protein in a 2 × 2 factorial design. Forty-four participants with complete pre- and post-intervention data were analyzed. Fasting blood samples were assessed for blood urea nitrogen (BUN), BUN/creatinine ratio, cystatin C, and eGFR calculated using the CKD-EPI creatinine (2021), cystatin C (2012), and creatinine-cystatin C (2021) equations. Within-group changes were evaluated using paired t-tests, and factorial effects were assessed using linear mixed-effects models (Time × Training × Protein).

Results

No statistically significant Time × Protein or Time × Training × Protein interactions were detected for any renal biomarker or eGFR estimate (all p ≥ 0.182). No significant within-group changes occurred in the 1.6 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ groups (all p > 0.05). In both 3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ groups, BUN and cystatin C increased (all p ≤ 0.017), while eGFR estimates decreased (all p ≤ 0.009). The BUN/creatinine ratio remained unchanged (p ≥ 0.614). However, these within-group findings were descriptive because the corresponding interaction effects were not statistically significant.

Conclusions

In resistance-trained men, 16 weeks of high protein intake did not produce statistically detectable differences in renal biomarker or eGFR changes compared with moderate protein intake, irrespective of training modality. Although modest increases in BUN and cystatin C and small decreases in eGFR estimates were observed within the high-protein groups, these findings were not supported by significant factorial interactions. The limited sample size precludes excluding clinically meaningful differences, warranting further investigation in larger studies.

records.title: An Automated Blood Flow Restriction Device Is Reliable, but Not Valid, for Determining Lower Limb Occlusion Pressure in Resistance-trained Adults.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: An Automated Blood Flow Restriction Device Is Reliable, but Not Valid, for Determining Lower Limb Occlusion Pressure in Resistance-trained Adults.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Lang, D, Fallo, X, and Bennett, H. An automated blood flow restriction device is reliable, but not valid, for determining lower limb occlusion pressure in resistance-trained adults. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Blood flow restriction (BFR) exercise can improve strength, hypertrophy, and aerobic performance. Accurate limb occlusion pressure (LOP) assessment is essential for safe prescription. The AirBands is a novel automated BFR device that estimates LOP using integrated sensors, making LOP assessment easier. However, its validity and reliability are not well established in resistance-trained individuals. This study evaluated the concurrent validity of the AirBands compared with a handheld Doppler ultrasound for lower limb LOP, and its test-retest reliability, in resistance-trained adults. Twenty-six resistance-trained adults (14 males, 12 females; 24.2 ± 4.7 years) participated. For validity, LOP was measured using AirBands and Doppler in randomized order, using the same cuff. For reliability, automated LOP was measured twice, 10 minutes apart. Agreement was assessed using Bland-Altman limits of agreement and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). No significant difference was observed between manual (231.7 ± 17.8 mm Hg) and automated (230.8 ± 38.3 mm Hg) LOP (mean difference -0.8 mm Hg; p = 0.928), although validity ICC was poor (0.236, 95% confidence interval [CI] = -0.293 to 0.641). Bland-Altman analysis indicated proportional bias, with overestimation at lower values and underestimation at higher values. Reliability showed no significant difference between test 1 (243.0 ± 37.5 mm Hg) and test 2 (242.3 ± 40.5 mm Hg) (mean difference 1.0 mm Hg; p = 0.816) and good reliability (ICC = 0.862, 95% CI = 0.715 to 0.936). AirBands demonstrates good test-retest reliability but poor concurrent validity vs. Doppler ultrasound. Clinicians should confirm automated values using a Doppler ultrasound before prescribing BFR.

records.title: Independent and joint associations of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep with vitamin D status in US adults: a cross-sectional NHANES study.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Independent and joint associations of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep with vitamin D status in US adults: a cross-sectional NHANES study.
content.abstract:
Background

Emerging evidence links movement behaviors to vitamin D status. This study investigated associations between physical activity (PA), sedentary behavior (SB), and sleep with vitamin D status and explored sex differences in these relationships.

Methods

This cross-sectional study included 3195 adults (49.1 ± 17.1 years, 45.5% males) from the 2021-2023 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey with complete data. Self-reported PA, SB, and sleep duration were assessed. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D was measured using high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Generalized linear and logistic regression models were performed.

Results

SB was negatively associated with vitamin D levels in the whole sample (β = -0.006; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.012, -0.001) and males (β = -0.008; 95% CI: -0.014, -0.002), but not females. Sleep duration was positively associated with vitamin D among males only (β = 0.023; 95% CI: 0.003, 0.043). Meeting both PA and SB guidelines showed the strongest and most consistent association with vitamin D sufficiency, observed across the whole sample (odds ratio [OR] = 2.129; 95% CI: 1.504, 3.012), males (OR = 2.013; 95% CI: 1.021, 3.967), and females (OR = 2.214; 95% CI: 1.360, 3.605).

Conclusions

Movement behaviors demonstrate independent and joint associations with vitamin D status in US adults, with modest sex-specific patterns that warrant replication. Combined adherence to PA and SB guidelines was consistently associated with greater odds of vitamin D sufficiency across sexes.

records.title: Effects of milk fat globule membrane supplementation on physical function and body composition in older adults: a narrative review.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of milk fat globule membrane supplementation on physical function and body composition in older adults: a narrative review.
content.abstract:
Background

Healthy aging is a priority for many individuals; however, a decline in physical function and poor body composition are common age-related changes that can cause the added years from rising life expectancy to be spent in poor health. Consequently, understanding the mechanisms involved in aging has become increasingly important, including the role of phospholipids (PLs) and how age-related changes in PL content may interfere with lipid metabolism and normal functioning of the musculoskeletal system. Milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) is a bovine milk fraction rich in PLs that may have the potential to support good physical health, so that quality of life can rise alongside life expectancy.

Methods

This narrative review was based on a literature search conducted on Google Scholar, PubMed, and Scopus in May 2026 using the following keywords and Boolean operators: milk fat globule membrane OR MFGM AND physical function OR body composition OR older adults. Studies were included if they were randomized clinical trials (RCTs) investigating MFGM's effects on physical function and/or body composition in older adults.

Results

Findings suggest that MFGM supplementation, when consumed in conjunction with exercise, is an effective way to improve physical function in older adults, particularly among Japanese cohorts; however, changes in habitual diet in response to exercise, variable PL concentrations, and other added ingredients used in interventions may have influenced these results. In contrast, its effects on body composition appear more modest, with some studies reporting no benefits, especially when exercise was not part of the study design, or when compliance may have been a factor.

Conclusions

Beyond the combined use of supplementation and exercise, future RCTs should consistently report participant compliance and, where possible, examine MFGM as a standalone intervention to distinguish its effects from other bioactive ingredients. Greater standardization is also needed, particularly regarding PL dose. Studies should also aim to include participants from more diverse ethnic backgrounds to capture a wider range of physiological responses and improve generalizability of the findings.

records.title: Effects of extremely low-volume high-intensity interval training combined with iron supplementation versus iron supplementation alone on postural control in young women with iron deficiency anemia: a randomized controlled trial.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of extremely low-volume high-intensity interval training combined with iron supplementation versus iron supplementation alone on postural control in young women with iron deficiency anemia: a randomized controlled trial.
content.abstract:
Background

Recent research revealed postural control deterioration in young women with Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA). To address this postural deficit, it is crucial to develop intervention strategies for postural rehabilitation in these individuals. This study aimed to explore the effect of 8-week extremely low-volume high-intensity interval training (HIIT) based on plyometric exercises combined with iron supplementation versus simple iron treatment on postural control of young women with IDA.

Methods

This randomized controlled trial enrolled young women with IDA aged 18-25 years, who were randomly assigned to a training group (TG; n = 16) or a non-training group (NTG; n = 17). All participants received oral iron supplementation (ferrous sulfate, 494.5 mg/day, administered as 247.25 mg twice daily), while the TG additionally completed an 8-week extremely low-volume HIIT program based on plyometric exercises. Hemoglobin (Hb) and serum ferritin concentrations were assessed, alongside muscle endurance, reaction time performance, and postural control. Muscle endurance was evaluated using the Killy test, reaction time performance using an online simple reaction time test, and postural control using a stabilometric platform under bipodal and semi-tandem stance conditions. Postural assessments were conducted with eyes open (EO) and eyes closed (EC) on firm and foam surfaces. All outcomes were measured at baseline and 72 h after the final intervention session.

Results

After the 8-week intervention, this study demonstrated significant improvements across both groups, irrespective of the intervention. However, TG showed significantly greater post-intervention improvements than NTG in Hb concentration (P = 0.042), muscle endurance (P < 0.001), and postural control. Superior postural control in TG was observed during a bipedal stance on a foam surface (EO: P = 0.001); EC: P = 0.035), as well as during semi-tandem stance on a firm surface (EO: P = 0.015; EC: P = 0.040) and on a foam surface (EO: P = 0.019; EC: P = 0.003), compared to the NTG. With a Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold for multiple comparisons (α = 0.00625), between-group differences in postural control remained significant for bipedal foam EO (P = 0.001) and semi-tandem foam EC (P = 0.003).

Conclusions

The study showed that women with IDA improved their postural performance regardless of the intervention used. However, an 8-week program of extremely low-volume HIIT combined with plyometric exercises and iron supplementation had a more beneficial effect compared to traditional iron therapy. These greater improvements in postural control occurred alongside greater improvements in the Hb concentration and muscle endurance in the TG compared to the NTG.

records.title: Acute and Chronic Effects of High-Load Resistance Training With Blood Flow Restriction in Healthy Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Acute and Chronic Effects of High-Load Resistance Training With Blood Flow Restriction in Healthy Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Mckee, JR, Raj, IS, Marston, KJ, De Marco, K, Beere, M, Galna, B, Peiffer, JJ, Nosaka, K, and Scott, BR. Acute and chronic effects of high-load resistance training with blood flow restriction in healthy adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res 40(7): 822-842, 2026-Blood flow restriction (BFR) improves muscle strength and size gains after low-load resistance training, though findings are conflicting for BFR with higher loads (≥60% of maximal strength). This systematic review with meta-analysis investigated whether high-load resistance training with BFR (a) further improves muscle size and strength and (b) increases acute performance, physiologic, and perceptual responses, when compared with conventional high-load resistance training. Six databases were searched to identify studies examining high-load resistance training with BFR in healthy adults. Risk of bias was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute appraisal tools. A multilevel meta-analysis using the inverse-variance weighted random effects model was conducted on muscle strength and size outcomes. Acute data were synthesized narratively. Eight chronic studies and 34 acute studies were included. Very-low certainty evidence indicates that high-load resistance training with BFR does not further improve muscle strength ( g = 0.11 [95% confidence intervals -0.11 to 0.33]) or size ( g = 0.08 [95% confidence intervals -0.18 to 0.34]) adaptations compared with conventional high-load resistance training. Acutely, high-load resistance exercise with BFR may increase concentric bar velocity without altering electromyography amplitude, cardiorespiratory, metabolic, and molecular responses. Findings regarding perceptual responses and the number of repetitions completed during high-load resistance exercise with BFR are conflicting. Current evidence suggests that adding BFR to high-load resistance training is not beneficial for enhancing muscle size and strength, likely because of comparable physiologic demands. However, the application of wide cuffs at high pressures may acutely increase concentric bar velocity that could be explored as a potential method for improving muscular power.

records.title: How Slow Should You Go? A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis of the Effect of Resistance Training Repetition Tempo on Muscle Hypertrophy.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: How Slow Should You Go? A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis of the Effect of Resistance Training Repetition Tempo on Muscle Hypertrophy.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Enes, A, Piñero, A, Hermann, T, Zamanzadeh, A, Hennessy, T, Montenegro, D, Parnell, C, Jia, A, Weitzman, T, Wolf, M, Korakakis, PA, Swinton, PA, and Schoenfeld, BJ. How slow should you go? A systematic review with meta-analysis of the effect of resistance training repetition tempo on muscle hypertrophy. J Strength Cond Res 39(12): 1331-1339, 2025-We systematically searched the literature for interventions that compared different resistance training tempos for eccentric (ECC) or concentric (CON) actions. We estimated pre-/poststudy changes and between-condition differences in lean/muscle mass for healthy adults, restricting inclusion to studies that controlled all other training variables. Hierarchical meta-analyses were conducted within a Bayesian framework, with change estimates made within groups, and the primary emphasis placed on pairwise differences between dichotomously coded slower (repetition time: 1.7-4.5 seconds, averaging ∼3.5 seconds) and faster (repetition time: 0.3-2 seconds, averaging ∼1 second) interventions. When combining data across all 14 included studies (4 CON and 9 ECC manipulated interventions, 1 for both in a cross-over design), meta-analyses of within-group changes showed similar pooled effects for faster (0.43 [95% CrI: 0.29‒0.58]) and slower tempos (0.34 [95% credible interval (CrI): 0.22‒0.47)]. Meta-analyses of pairwise differences across the same studies showed central estimates that trivially favored faster over slower tempos (pooled mean = 0.09 [95% CrI: -0.04 to 0.22]), with a low probability that the between-condition effect size was at least small (p = 0.450), medium (p = 0.001), or large (p < 0.001). Subgroup analyses of pairwise differences stratified by muscle action type (ECC or CON), body region (upper or lower body), and training to failure (yes or no) generally produced trivial to small effects, although the certainty of estimates varied across analyses. In conclusion, resistance training tempo appears to have minimal overall effect on muscle hypertrophy, with potential differences emerging under specific conditions.

records.title: Optimising exercise prescription for cancer-related fatigue, lean mass, physical function and muscle strength in women with breast cancer: a systematic review with dose-response network meta-analysis.

content.title: Optimising exercise prescription for cancer-related fatigue, lean mass, physical function and muscle strength in women with breast cancer: a systematic review with dose-response network meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

To systematically review and investigate the dose-response (DR) relationship of aerobic exercise (AE), resistance exercise (RE) and combined (COMB) exercise programmes on cancer-related fatigue, lean mass, physical function and muscle strength in women with breast cancer during and following primary treatment.

Design

Systematic review with DR network meta-analysis (DR-NMA; CRD42023491118).

Data sources

CINAHL, Embase, LILACS, PubMed, SciELO, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science were searched from inception to 10 January 2024, with an updated search in April 2025.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Randomised controlled trials evaluating COMB, RE or AE in women with breast cancer on the four specified outcomes.

Results

64 trials (n=5156) were included. COMB was the most effective modality for improving fatigue and lean mass, and RE was the most effective for improving physical function and muscle strength. The smallest effective doses of COMB associated with significant changes in fatigue (standardised mean differences (SMD) 0.23 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.28)) and lean mass (SMD 0.30 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.38)) were 18 and 11 metabolic equivalents per week (METs.min/week), respectively. For RE, about 7-8 METs.min/week produced significant improvements in physical function (SMD 0.23 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.30)) and strength (SMD 0.24 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.29)). Fatigue benefits (SMD 0.58 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.69)) plateaued at ~1428 METs.min/week for COMB, whereas no plateau was observed for lean mass or strength across the evaluated dose range, with effects increasing throughout the available dose range.

Conclusions

COMB and RE were the most effective interventions across outcomes in women with breast cancer. Benefits for the outcomes assessed in this systematic review with DR-NMA were achieved with exercise doses as low as 10-40 min/week.

records.title: The Impact of Aquatic Training on Athletic Performance and Physical Recovery in Competitive Athletes: A Meta-Analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: The Impact of Aquatic Training on Athletic Performance and Physical Recovery in Competitive Athletes: A Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Zheng, S, Wang, S, Cao, Q, and Li, H. The impact of aquatic training on athletic performance and physical recovery in competitive athletes: A meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res 40(6): 723-737, 2026-To evaluate the effects of aquatic training on performance and physical recovery in competitive athletes, particularly its impact on explosive power, speed, agility, strength, aerobic capacity, and balance. This study used a meta-analysis approach to search relevant literature in the Web of Science and Scopus databases since their inception. The selected studies were limited to English-language articles that met predefined inclusion criteria. All included studies were randomized controlled trials or controlled experiments, with subjects being competitive athletes with a systematic training background. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) were used for data analysis, and statistical analysis was conducted using R (version 4.3.0). A total of 13 studies were included in the analysis, with 392 subjects. Aquatic training significantly improved athletes' explosive power (SMD = 0.79, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.0.50 to 1.07, p < 0.001), speed (SMD = 1.14, 95% CI = 0.89 to 1.38, p < 0.001), and agility (SMD = 0.47, 95% CI = 0.0.15 to 0.78, p = 0.004). However, the improvement in strength (SMD = 0.32, 95% CI = -0.32 to 0.96, p = 0.321) and balance (SMD = 0.42, 95% CI = -0.35 to 1.19, p = 0.282) was not statistically significant, and there was high heterogeneity in the studies on aerobic capacity (SMD = 1.92, 95% CI = -1.47 to 5.32, p = 0.267). In addition, aquatic training showed a modest yet positive effect on physical recovery, including improvements related to injury rehabilitation and fatigue relief (SMD = 0.38, 95% CI = 0.12 to 0.63, p = 0.004). As an effective supplementary training method, aquatic training significantly enhances athletic performance, especially in explosive power, speed, and agility. It has beneficial effects on injury recovery and post-training fatigue reduction. Although the effects on strength and aerobic capacity require further validation, aquatic training has proven to be an important tool in sports training and rehabilitation with promising application potential.

records.title: Do blood flow restriction exercises offer additional benefits when compared to conventional exercises in musculoskeletal rehabilitation? A systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Do blood flow restriction exercises offer additional benefits when compared to conventional exercises in musculoskeletal rehabilitation? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objectives

This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy of low-load exercise with blood flow restriction (LLE-BFR) compared with low-load exercise (LLE) and high-load exercise (HLE) in individuals with musculoskeletal (MSK) conditions on muscle strength, disability and pain intensity.

Method

Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials (RCTs). Methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database (PEDro) scale and the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool.

Data source

Six databases were searched without language restrictions from inception to November 2025, with additional studies identified from reference lists.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

RCTs evaluating LLE-BFR versus LLE or HLE on muscle strength, pain intensity, disability and adverse events in people with MSK conditions.

Results

We included 45 RCTs (1652 participants), with 44 RCTs (1607 participants) contributing to meta-analyses (mean PEDro score=6.55; most of the included trials were rated as 'some concerns' across one or more RoB 2 domains). Low-certainty evidence indicated LLE-BFR was superior to LLE for muscle strength (standardised mean difference (SMD)=0.82, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.23) and disability (SMD=0.63, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.89). Moderate-certainty evidence showed no clear difference between LLE-BFR and HLE for muscle strength (SMD=0.08, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.35), and very-low certainty evidence showed no clear difference for disability (SMD=0.66, 95% CI -0.16 to 1.47). Moderate- and low-certainty evidence indicated small, unimportant differences favouring LLE-BFR over LLE (MD=4.45, 95% CI 1.21 to 7.71) and HLE (MD=7.71, 95% CI 1.62 to 13.8) for pain intensity, respectively. Very-low and low-certainty evidence suggested no difference in adverse events between LLE-BFR and LLE (risk ratio, RR=0.92) or HLE (RR=1.08); however, adverse-event monitoring and reporting were inconsistent across trials.

Conclusion

Low-certainty evidence indicates that LLE-BFR improves muscle strength and disability compared with LLE. Moderate-certainty evidence showed no clear difference in muscle strength compared with HLE, while evidence for disability was very low certainty, precluding firm conclusions. Prediction intervals were wide for several outcomes. Although pain reductions favoured LLE-BFR, these effects were small and unlikely to be clinically meaningful, and evidence regarding adverse events remains limited.

records.title: Effects of supervised exercise during pregnancy on gestational diabetes mellitus and other pregnancy outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Effects of supervised exercise during pregnancy on gestational diabetes mellitus and other pregnancy outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

To evaluate the effects of supervised exercise on gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) and other pregnancy outcomes and examine dose-response relationships.

Design

Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression.

Data sources

Four databases were searched up to November 2025.

Eligibility criteria

Randomised controlled trials in pregnant women comparing supervised exercise with usual care were included if they reported GDM. GDM was prespecified as the primary outcome, while other outcomes were extracted where available, including gestational hypertension (GH), pre-eclampsia, excessive gestational weight gain (EGWG), macrosomia, caesarean delivery, preterm birth and low birth weight.

Results

Nineteen studies (n=6213; 48.6% in intervention groups) were included, with moderate certainty of evidence. Supervised exercise reduced the risk of GDM (risk ratio (RR) 0.74, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.96; I2=47%), GH (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.77; I2=1%), EGWG (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.92; I2=70%) and macrosomia (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.81; I2=27%). Subgroup analyses for these outcomes suggested greater effects with earlier intervention (initiated in early pregnancy or duration >20 weeks), higher adherence (≥80%), combined aerobic and resistance training, and weekly exercise duration ≥150 min/week. Significant subgroup differences in GDM risk were observed for intervention initiation timing (p=0.009) and intervention duration (p=0.010). Dose-response analysis showed a peak effect at approximately 500-550 metabolic equivalent task-minutes per week for EGWG, with a plateau at higher doses.

Conclusion

Supervised exercise during pregnancy reduces adverse pregnancy outcomes when initiated early, with high adherence, at moderate doses, and with combined aerobic and resistance training.

records.title: Effectiveness and feasibility of home-based physical exercise interventions for children and adolescents with chronic diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Effectiveness and feasibility of home-based physical exercise interventions for children and adolescents with chronic diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

(1) To synthesise the available evidence on the clinical effectiveness of home-based physical exercise interventions in improving aerobic capacity, functional capacity, muscle strength and quality of life in children and adolescents with chronic diseases, as well as to evaluate their feasibility; and (2) to assess the reporting quality of these interventions using the Consensus on Exercise Reporting Template, with the aim of identifying gaps in methodological transparency that may limit reproducibility and scalability.

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis.

Data sources

Medline (via PubMed), Web of Science, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), SportDiscus and CINAHL database (via EBSCOhost) were searched until 31 December 2025.

Eligibility criteria

Eligible studies included intervention designs (randomised controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomised trials and before-after studies) that evaluated home-based physical exercise interventions in children and adolescents with chronic diseases. Studies were required to include a comparator (eg, centre-based interventions, alternative home-based interventions, such as motor imagery, constraint-induced movement therapy or hand-arm bimanual intensive therapy or no intervention) or to report within-group (baseline-to-follow-up) comparisons. Outcomes of interest were aerobic capacity, functional capacity, muscle strength and quality of life.

Results

A total of 81 studies were included, comprising 2923 children and adolescents. The most frequently represented conditions were cerebral palsy (n=26; 32.1%), cystic fibrosis (n=10; 12.3%) and idiopathic arthritis (n=8; 9.8%). Of the 45 RCTs identified, 19 met the criteria for inclusion in the meta-analysis. Home-based physical exercise interventions were effective in increasing aerobic capacity (p<0.0001; standardised mean differences: 0.53; 95% CI 0.32 to 0.74) compared with the control group. No significant differences were observed between home-based interventions and control conditions for functional capacity or quality of life. However, functional capacity gains are similar when comparing centre-based and home-based approaches. A meta-analysis of muscle strength could not be performed due to insufficient data. Adherence to home-based physical exercise interventions was higher than 80% in 27 of the 50 studies that reported this information. Most studies reported no adverse events of home-based physical exercise interventions, with few studies reporting only mild adverse effects (eg, muscle soreness, stiffness and fatigue).

Conclusions

Our meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials comparing home-based interventions with control conditions suggests that home-based physical exercise is feasible and improves aerobic capacity, but does not confer significant benefits for functional capacity, muscle strength or quality of life in children and adolescents with chronic diseases. Suboptimal reporting quality, risk of bias and inconsistent adherence/safety data necessitate cautious interpretation.

records.title: Effects of dietary supplements on lower-limb power and jump performance in physically active individuals and athletes: a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of dietary supplements on lower-limb power and jump performance in physically active individuals and athletes: a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

To evaluate the relative effects of dietary supplements, the certainty of evidence, and the robustness of findings within separate networks for peak power (PP), relative peak power (RPP), vertical jump (VJ), and countermovement jump (CMJ).

Methods

PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were systematically searched, with the final search conducted on September 8, 2026. Eligible studies were randomised parallel-group and crossover controlled trials published in English through August 31, 2026, involving healthy individuals with physical activity or training backgrounds. Four separate Bayesian random-effects networks were constructed. Effects were assessed using mean differences (MDs) in change scores, 95% credible intervals (CrIs), and prediction intervals. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using RoB 2 and CINeMA, respectively. Subgroup analyses, network meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses were also conducted. This review was retrospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261283835).

Results

A total of 119 studies were included. The PP, RPP, VJ, and CMJ networks comprised 47, 33, 31, and 44 studies, respectively, with some studies contributing to more than one outcome. Compared with placebo, β-hydroxy-β-methylbutyrate (HMB) yielded MDs of 64.70 W (95% CrI: 19.15 to 110.50) for PP and 0.84 W·kg-1 (95% CrI: 0.42 to 1.28) for RPP. Favourable effects were also observed for β-alanine on PP and for creatine and vitamin D on RPP. Iron supplementation yielded an MD of 6.81 cm (95% CrI: 0.84 to 12.83) for VJ, supported by only one direct study. For CMJ, betaine yielded an MD of 3.72 cm (95% CrI: 1.24 to 6.18); the 95% CrIs for palmitoylethanolamide, caffeine combined with Rhodiola rosea, creatine, multi-ingredient supplements, and caffeine also excluded zero. The HMB findings for RPP remained relatively stable across multiple sensitivity analyses, whereas some other favourable comparisons had prediction intervals that included zero or showed attenuated findings in sensitivity analyses. Exploratory associations with training level and sport were observed for RPP, although interpretation was limited by sparse evidence and imbalanced covariate distributions. Of 1,636 pairwise comparisons, 17 were rated as moderate, 55 as low, and 1,564 as very low certainty. The HMB-versus-placebo comparisons for both PP and RPP were rated as moderate certainty.

Conclusions
