Some supplements showed favourable effects within their respective networks, with the HMB findings for RPP remaining relatively stable. However, direct evidence was limited, and the certainty of evidence was very low for most comparisons. Findings should be interpreted in the context of the populations and supplementation regimens studied. Differences between networks cannot establish that outcome type modifies supplementation effects, and rankings alone should not be used to guide individualised supplementation regimens.

records.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews.
content.abstract:
Purpose

The aim of this overview of reviews was to determine the impact of resistance training (RT) prescription on muscle function and hypertrophy, utilizing evidence synthesis methods. It updates the American College of Sports Medicine 2009 Position Stand, "Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults."

Data sources

Ovid MEDLINE(R) ALL, Ovid Emcare, Ovid Embase, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, EBSCOhost SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science Core Collection current to October 2024.

Eligibility criteria

Eligible systematic reviews synthesized randomized trials of healthy adults (≥18 yr) who completed RT (≥6 wk; range: 6-52 wk), compared with a group that completed no exercise or an alternative RT program, and reported the change in muscle function, size, or physical performance.

Results

We synthesized data from 137 systematic reviews (>30,000 participants). Compared with no exercise (control), RT significantly improved muscle strength, size (hypertrophy), power, endurance, contraction velocity, gait speed, balance, and multiple physical function outcomes. Few RT prescription (RTx) variables affected primary adaptations. However, voluntary strength was enhanced by lifting heavier loads (≥80% one-repetition maximum), through a complete range of motion, for 2-3 sets, at the beginning of training sessions, and ≥2 sessions/wk. Muscle hypertrophy was enhanced by higher volumes (≥10 sets/wk) and eccentric overload. Power was enhanced by moderate loads (30%-70% one-repetition maximum), low-to-moderate volume (≤24 repetitions⋅sets), Olympic-style weightlifting, and power RT (fast concentric phase). Power RT enhanced physical function. Training to momentary muscle fatigue, equipment type, exercise complexity, set structure, time under tension, blood flow restriction, and periodization did not consistently impact training outcomes.

Conclusions

Healthy adults should perform progressive RT, with variable prescription consistent with our findings, to improve muscle function, size, and physical performance. Muscle strength, hypertrophy, power, and certain components of physical function can be enhanced by manipulating the RT variables highlighted.

records.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: diets for body weight reduction.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: diets for body weight reduction.
content.abstract: The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) has developed an official position on diets for body weight reduction. This critical analysis of the literature is intended to provide a scientific foundation for practitioners, coaches, and trainees regarding the effects of the major diet types in adults who are generally healthy, physically active, and/or athletic, while drawing from clinical research in those with overweight/obesity, when relevant. This position stand does not address acute dehydration-based weight cutting, pharmacotherapy (i.e. GLP-1RAs), or bariatric surgery. The following 15 points constitute the Position Statement of the Society; the Research Committee has approved them. 1) Diets for body weight reduction can be broadly categorized by the magnitude of the energy deficit, linearity of the deficit, and macronutrient composition. These factors need to be tailored to individual preferences, tolerances, and goals.2) Very-low-energy diets (<800 kcal/day) and low-energy diets (800-1200  kcal/day) produce greater short-term weight loss but lack long-term advantages over less aggressive energy restrictions, such as calorie-controlled diets. These aggressive diets may increase lean mass loss, although adequate protein intake and resistance training may mitigate this risk. Caution is warranted about insufficiencies in vitamins, minerals, fiber, and other nutrients.3) The evidence at-large shows a lack of differential effects between intermittent fasting variants (alternate-day fasting, time-restricted eating, and twice-weekly fasting) and continuous energy restriction on anthropometric outcomes, although macronutrient quality plays an independent role in optimizing body composition and metabolic health.4) Intra-day meal frequency (as opposed to total daily nutrition) does not tend to crucially influence body weight and body fat reduction. Meal frequency may be individualized flexibly; no lower or upper limits can universally be prescribed to optimize outcomes. However, in physically active and athletic populations, distributing protein across at least three protein-rich meals (or eating occasions) per day may optimize lean mass retention and performance during sustained energy deficits.5) Resistance training and sufficient protein intake are indispensable mitigators of lean mass loss in a sustained caloric deficit, regardless of the diet type or variant. Total daily protein is of primary importance; specific distribution of the constituent doses is a secondary concern.6) For the general population, a daily protein intake of 1.2-1.6 g/kg BW is appropriate for supporting total body weight and fat loss, physical activity, and imparting benefits to musculoskeletal and cardiometabolic health.7) Daily protein intakes ranging 1.6-2.2 g/kg BW combined with resistance training may optimize muscle anabolism, while higher intakes of 1.9-3.2 g/kg BW can maximize lean mass retention in lean, resistance-trained individuals sustaining hypocaloric conditions.8) The dietary carbohydrate‒fat proportion can be individualized to personal preference for the goal of weight loss, since the range of ketogenic to low-fat diets performs similarly.9) Ketogenic diets are effective at bodyweight and body fat reduction, but they also tend to decrease fat-free mass to a greater degree than higher-carbohydrate comparators, particularly in shorter trials where glycogen and total body water shifts can influence estimates.10) Adaptations to weight loss can be physical, physiological, and/or behavioral, and converge toward reducing energy expenditure to fulfill the body's drive toward neutralizing disruptions to homeostasis imposed by the caloric deficit.11) Adaptive thermogenesis is a reduction in resting energy expenditure beyond that predicted by changes in body composition. It can occur in response to hypocaloric conditions and weight loss, but it is not an inevitable response, and it may attenuate substantially upon attainment of weight stability.12) Metabolic adaptations that reduce energy expenditure, including adaptive thermogenesis, and impair gut microbial diversity, can often be attenuated by strategic dietary and exercise programming that foster nutrient-absorption and partitioning, and metabolic flexibility.13) A multitude of tactics can be implemented to manage and overcome plateaus. However, plateaus are also opportunities/cues to practice maintaining progress made thus far (the ultimate goal is the maintenance of a plateau).14) Guidance from an interdisciplinary team of health professionals while maintaining social support is recommended for successful weight management.15) Learning how to prepare home-cooked meals (and plan meals ahead of time through the day) puts dieters in control of their nutritional fate - and in a better position to succeed in managing their body weight and body composition.

records.title: Impact of different protein sources on acute muscle protein synthesis following resistance training: a systematic review with standard and dose-response network meta-analyses.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Impact of different protein sources on acute muscle protein synthesis following resistance training: a systematic review with standard and dose-response network meta-analyses.
content.abstract:
Background

The combination of protein intake and resistance training (RT) plays a pivotal role in stimulating muscle protein synthesis (MPS), yet the impact of different protein sources remains an area of active investigation. Therefore, a systematic review incorporating standard and dose‒response network meta-analyses was performed.

Methods

Systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, EBSCOhost (including MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL), and Scopus. Eligible studies included healthy adults (≥18 years) who were undergoing acute resistance exercise followed by a single protein bolus (any type or dose, except blends or enriched with anabolic agents). Muscle biopsies were required before and after RT/protein intake without additional food in between. Trials measuring hourly MPS rates via tracer techniques were included (n = 51).

Results

In the standard network meta-analysis (NMA), native whey (P-score = 0.81, MD = 0.05% [0.00; 0.10]), pea protein (0.77, MD = 0.05% [-0.02; 0.11]), whole egg protein (0.72, MD = 0.04% [-0.01; 0.09]), mycoprotein (0.66, MD = 0.03% [-0.02; 0.08]), and whey protein (0.58, MD = 0.02% [0.01; 0.04]) ranked highest for estimated efficacy in stimulating post-RT hourly MPS (in descending order) (only whey protein showed a statistically significant effect) with low to moderate certainty of evidence. Dose‒response NMA revealed that certain animal- (native whey and whole egg protein) and plant- (pea and mycoprotein) based protein sources to show the highest predicted MPS responses with doses of 18-25 g.

Conclusions

Animal- (native whey, whey, whole egg) and plant-based (pea, mycoprotein) proteins ranked similarly for estimated acute MPS stimulation when combined with RT; however, only whey protein showed a statistically significant effect, and protein sources represented by few studies should be interpreted with caution.

records.title: Effects of exercise on metabolic risk, cardiovascular fitness, and body composition in elderly women of the past decade: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of exercise on metabolic risk, cardiovascular fitness, and body composition in elderly women of the past decade: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Age-related reductions in physical activity and unfavorable body composition changes promote metabolic dysfunction and cardiovascular risk elevation in older populations. Due to estrogen-related factors, differences in cardiovascular risks, and musculoskeletal conditions, exercise may be one of the most accessible and widely applicable lifestyle interventions for older women. A comprehensive and systematic search has not yet been carried out on the effects of exercise on cardiovascular risk and its related indicators in elderly women. This meta-analysis evaluates exercise effects on metabolic risk, cardiovascular health, and body composition in healthy elderly women.

Methods

Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, CNKI, VIP, Wanfang, and Sinomed (2014-2024) for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing supervised exercise with nonexercise controls. Data were analyzed with fixed- and random-effect models in Stata 17.0. The Cochrane RoB2 tool assessed bias risk, while the certainty of evidence was evaluated through the GRADE approach.

Results

Twenty-three RCTs (33 intervention arms, 23 controls) were included. Exercise significantly reduced triglycerides (TG) (-8.56 mg/dL, 95% CI: -16.72, -0.40), total cholesterol (TC)(-26.67 mg/dL, 95% CI: -34.92, -18.42), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) (-23.77 mg/dL, 95% CI: -34.48, -13.05), blood glucose (Glu) (-5.59 mg/dL, 95% CI: -10.12, -1.06), and C-reactive protein (CRP) (-0.86 mg/L, 95% CI: -1.37, -0.35). Cardiovascular improvements included increased VO2peak (+2.78 mL/kg/min, 95% CI: 1.87, 3.70) and reduced systolic blood pressure (SBP) (-8.35 mmHg) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) (-3.26 mmHg). Regarding body composition, relative body fat (RF, i.e. body fat percentage) decreased (-2.47%, 95% CI: -3.42, -1.53), but no significant changes were observed in body weight, trunk fat mass (TFM), waist circumference (WC), fat-free mass (FFM), or skeletal muscle mass (SMM). According to the GRADE framework, the evidence was of moderate certainty for reductions in TC, TG, RF, VO₂peak, and SBP; and low certainty for all other outcomes.

Conclusion

This meta-analysis provides evidence that appropriate exercise (aerobic, resistance, combined exercise) effectively reduces cardiovascular risk factors in elderly women via dual mechanisms of body composition remodeling and metabolic homeostasis enhancement, with particular efficacy in lipid regulation and blood pressure control.

records.title: The effectiveness of protein supplements on athletic performance and post-exercise recovery - a Bayesian multilevel meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: The effectiveness of protein supplements on athletic performance and post-exercise recovery - a Bayesian multilevel meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Background

Protein supplements are a popular category of dietary supplements among fitness enthusiasts and athletes. However, research providing definitive conclusions on the effects of protein on athletic performance and post-exercise recovery remains limited. Key factors, such as protein source, timing, and optimal dosage, require further investigation to clarify their impact.

Method

A systematic search across seven databases identified 6,129 studies, which were screened using the Covidence online tool. After independent selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment by two reviewers, 75 studies involving 1,206 athletes were included in the meta-analysis. A multilevel meta-analysis synthesized data from the included studies using a Bayesian hierarchical model with the brms package. Publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot generated with the PublicationBias package and by calculating the P value of Egger's test through the metafor package. Additionally, a moderation analysis with the brms package was conducted to examine the relationship between seven moderators and effect sizes.

Results

The results demonstrated that the effects of protein-carbohydrate supplements showed statistical significance in comparison to the placebo group [μ(SMD): 0.57, 95% CI: 0.2 to 0.93] in enhancing endurance performance. Pure protein supplements demonstrated statistically significant effects compared to the placebo group in both endurance performance [μ(SMD): 0.37, 95% CI: 0.02 to 0.71] and muscle strength [μ(SMD): 0.72, 95% CI: 0.18 to 1.27]. For post-exercise recovery, pure protein supplements also showed statistically significant effects compared to carbohydrate supplements for maintaining glycogen resynthesis [μ(SMD): 0.83, 95% CI: 0.21 to 1.46]. However, the results indicated that all significant effects were observed in randomized controlled trials where the energy intake between the intervention and control groups was not matched.

Conclusion

The effects of protein supplementation on athletic performance and post-exercise recovery appear to be limited. Protein supplements showed beneficial effects compared to no supplementation. However, all statistically significant results were derived from studies in which energy intake was not matched between groups. This suggests that the observed benefits may not be attributable to protein per se. An additional intake of 1 g/kg/day of protein from supplements, resulting in a total daily protein intake of approximately 2 g/kg/day, appears to be most effective for enhancing athletic performance.

Registration

Registered at the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) (identification code CRD42024608194).

records.title: The Association Between Athletic Movement Quality and Physical Fitness in Athletic Populations: A Systematic Review With Multilevel Meta-Analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: The Association Between Athletic Movement Quality and Physical Fitness in Athletic Populations: A Systematic Review With Multilevel Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Wijekulasuriya, GA, Woods, CT, Kittel, A, and Larkin, P. The association between athletic movement quality and physical fitness in athletic populations: A systematic review with multilevel meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res 40(11): 1449-1465, 2026-Proficient athletic movement skill is purported to be foundational for the development of physical fitness qualities. Conducting a meta-analysis to determine the association between athletic movement quality and physical fitness in athletic populations would thus provide empirical evidence to substantiate or challenge this purportion. The aim of this study was to undertake a systematic review and meta-analysis to determine the association between athletic movement quality and physical fitness measures in athletic populations. Following our literature search, 62 studies were identified for inclusion. Multilevel meta-analyses were then conducted to determine the association between assessments of athletic movement quality and physical fitness measures, which included GRADE assessments for certainty of evidence. Subgroup analysis determined whether associations differed between movement quality assessments. There was high certainty of evidence for the association between athletic movement quality and balance, lower-body bilateral power, and speed. There were also associations between athletic movement quality and cardiorespiratory endurance, flexibility, and muscular strength. However, associations were negligible to low in magnitude and were assessment-dependent for some physical fitness measures. Bias due to nonreporting and limited control for confounding factors was identified, and moderate model and between-study heterogeneity was evident for most meta-analyses. Thus, the association between athletic movement quality and physical fitness seems small and assessment specific. These results may influence the selection of athletic movement quality assessments for athletes in addition to long-term athletic development strategies in youth populations.

records.title: The Road to Designing Integrated Neuromuscular Training Programs for Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: The Road to Designing Integrated Neuromuscular Training Programs for Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Li, M, Crotti, M, Martins, R, Tiernan, C, Lyons, M, Lander, N, Barnett, LM, and Duncan, MJ. The road to designing integrated neuromuscular training programs for children and adolescents: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res 39(10): 1105-1122, 2025-Integrative neuromuscular training (INT) combines motor competence and strength development to boost athletic performance, but its specific components and effects on children and adolescents are not well understood. Three predetermined principles (INT exercise categories, INT progression modalities, and INT program effectiveness) were used to guide this review. Electronic databases SPORTDiscus, MEDLINE (Ovid), APA PsycINFO, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Embase were searched. Search terms related to study design, population, and intervention were identified, and risk of bias was appraised using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database (PEDro) Scale. Narrative synthesis indicated "strength training" (18 out of 30 studies, 60%), particularly core strength exercises (72.2%), was the most common in INT exercise categories. Twelve out of 30 studies (40%) met at least 2 types of INT progression modalities (i.e., volume-based progressions, intensity-based progressions, and complexity-oriented progressions). Meta-analysis reported significant improvements in countermovement jump (mean difference [MD] 3.32 cm, 95% CI [2.07, 4.38]; p = 0.00), push-up (MD 3.74 repetitions, 95% CI [1.53, 5.95]; p = 0.00), and sprint (standardized MD -0.18 s, 95% CI [-0.26 to -0.09]; p = 0.00), but not in flexibility. Subgroup analysis revealed that meeting all the 3 progression modalities significantly enhanced sprint (standardized MD -0.76 s, 95% CI [1.21 to -0.31]; p = 0.03) and flexibility (MD 6.38 cm, 95% CI [5.45 to 7.31]; p = 0.00). This review provides evidence that INT programs have a positive effect on improving children and adolescents' physical fitness and is regarded as a promising protocol. This review and future research can inform a call to action for using INT as a novel approach for developing motor competence, strength, and conditioning simultaneously during childhood and adolescence.

records.title: Comparative Efficacy of Various Exercise Modes on Inflammatory Markers in Patients with Heart Failure: A Pairwise and Network Meta-Analysis.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Comparative Efficacy of Various Exercise Modes on Inflammatory Markers in Patients with Heart Failure: A Pairwise and Network Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Introduction/purpose

The aim of this systematic review with pairwise and network meta-analyses was to identify the most effective exercise mode for reducing proinflammatory markers in patients with heart failure (HF).

Methods

A systematic electronic search was carried out in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from inception to June 2024 in English-language publications. Randomized trials investigating the effect of any mode of exercise training, including aerobic training, resistance training (RT), combined training (CT), or Tai Chi/Yoga on proinflammatory markers, including IL-6, TNF-α, or CRP in patients with HF with reduced or preserved left-ventricular ejection fraction were included. Standardized mean differences and 95% confidence intervals were determined using random-effects models for meta-analyses.

Results

A total of 21 studies involving 1022 patients with HF were included. Overall, compared with controls (CON), exercise training was significantly more effective for reducing IL-6 (SMD -0.33, 95% CI -0.56 to -0.11, P = 0.003), TNF-α (SMD -0.17, 95% CI -0.34 to -0.00, P = 0.04), and CRP (SMD -0.57, 95% CI -1.02 to -0.13, P = 0.01). Particularly, RT (SMD -0.91, 95% CI -1.32 to -0.49, P = 0.001) and Tai Chi/Yoga (SMD -0.70, 95% CI -1.22 to -0.19, P = 0.006) were the most effective modality for reducing IL-6, CT (SMD -0.44, 95% CI -0.80 to -0.09, P = 0.01) and aerobic training (SMD -0.25, 95% CI -0.49 to 0.01, P = 0.03) were the optimal modality for lowering TNF-α, and CT (SMD -1.34, 95% CI -2.28 to -0.40, P = 0.004) was the optimal modality for lowering CRP.

Conclusions

Exercise training may contribute to improvements in chronic low-grade inflammation in patients with HF. RT is likely to be the most effective exercise mode for reducing IL-6, while of the exercise modalities studied, CT was optimal for lowering TNF-α and CRP. These findings should, however, be interpreted with caution owing to heterogeneity and the limited number of studies.

records.title: Comparison of Variable Resistance and Free Weight Training on Long-Term and Acute Effects on Different Assessments of Strength: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Comparison of Variable Resistance and Free Weight Training on Long-Term and Acute Effects on Different Assessments of Strength: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Li, J, Chen, Z, Xu, K, Wang, Y, and Gong, M. Comparison of variable resistance and free weight training on long-term and acute effects on different assessments of strength: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res 40(2): e211-e223, 2026-Variable resistance training (VRT) addresses biomechanical disadvantages of free weight training (FWT), but its long-term and acute effects on strength remain underexplored. This study aimed to compare the effects of VRT and FWT on the following variables-maximal strength, velocity, power output, and jump distance-under both long-term and acute interventions. The study used cluster analysis to define variable resistance load proportion (VRLP) groups. Pairwise meta-analysis assessed long-term outcomes, subgroup analyses by VRLP, VRT equipment (elastic bands or chains), and number of VRT exercises (single or multiple). Acute interventions were evaluated using network meta-analysis across VRLP and FWT groups. Effect sizes were reported as standardized mean differences (SMD). For long-term effects, VRT outperformed FWT in maximal strength (repetition maximum or force output) and jump distance (vertical or horizontal) (0.28 ≤ SMD ≤ 0.37). Specifically, chain-based loading and VRLP ≤20% showed advantages across both outcomes (0.39 ≤ SMD ≤ 0.51). Multiple-exercise VRT improved maximal strength (SMD = 0.27), whereas single-exercise VRT improved jump distance (SMD = 0.46). For acute effects, VRLP >20% showed superior maximal strength (force output) (0.46 ≤ SMD ≤ 0.79), VRLP >37% resulted in lower maximal velocity (movement velocity) and power output (SMD ≤ -1.31) compared with FWT. Thus, long-term VRT surpasses FWT in maximal strength and jump distance, with chain-based or VRLP ≤20% of VRT optimal; multiple exercises benefit maximal strength, and single exercise improves maximal jump distance. Acutely, VRLP of 21-37% VRT results in greater mechanical output in a variety of exercises.

records.title: Effects of different exercise training modalities on 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure in adults with hypertension: a network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.

content.title: Effects of different exercise training modalities on 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure in adults with hypertension: a network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Objective

To compare the effects of exercise training modalities on 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure in adults with hypertension.

Design

Systematic review and network meta-analysis.

Data sources

MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central and Regional Portal of the Virtual Health Library were systematically searched from November 2024 to August 2025.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Randomised controlled trials evaluating the effects of exercise training (intervention duration ≥4 weeks) compared with a non-exercise control condition or another exercise modality on 24-hour systolic and diastolic blood pressure were included.

Results

31 trials were included, with 67 arms and 1345 participants. In the network meta-analysis, compared with the control, combined training (mean difference (MD) -6.18 mm Hg, 95% credible interval (CrI) -11.45 to -1.21), aerobic training (MD -4.73 mm Hg, 95% CrI -7.53 to -2.01), and high-intensity interval training (MD -5.71 mm Hg, 95% CrI -11.31 to -0.002) reduced 24-hour systolic blood pressure. Reductions in 24-hour diastolic blood pressure were observed with combined training (MD -3.94, 95% CrI -6.47 to -1.34), aerobic training (MD -2.76, 95% CrI -4.21 to -1.34), high-intensity interval training (MD -4.64, 95% CrI -8.21 to -0.72) and pilates (MD -4.18, 95% CrI -7.18 to -1.17). Exercise-versus-exercise comparisons were inconclusive with respect to superiority between modalities.

Conclusion

Aerobic training (continuous and interval) and combined training significantly reduced 24-hour blood pressure. Evidence for dynamic and isometric resistance training remains uncertain. Data on non-conventional exercise modalities such as pilates and recreational sports are limited and imprecise for the management of ambulatory blood pressure.

records.title: The Effect of Strength Training on Endurance Performance Determinants in Middle- and Long-Distance Endurance Athletes: An Umbrella Review of Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: The Effect of Strength Training on Endurance Performance Determinants in Middle- and Long-Distance Endurance Athletes: An Umbrella Review of Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Ramos-Campo, DJ, Andreu Caravaca, L, Clemente-Suárez, VJ, and Rubio-Arias, JÁ. The effect of strength training on endurance performance determinants in middle- and long-distance endurance athletes: An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res 39(4): 492-506, 2025-Strength training is used to enhance endurance performance in middle- and long-distance endurance athletes. However, likely due to heterogeneity and the variety of training methodologies used, not all studies have found improvements in endurance performance with the incorporation of strength training. We aimed to review the available systematic reviews and meta-analytical evidence examining the effects of strength training on endurance performance factors in endurance-trained athletes. An umbrella review was conducted. Strength training programs were categorized into (a) maximal-strength training (>80% 1-Repetition Maximum [1RM]), (b) explosive-strength training (<80% 1RM), and (c) reactive-strength training (plyometric training). Male and/or female middle-to long-distance endurance-trained athletes were included. Variables analyzed were maximum oxygen uptake (V̇o2max), endurance performance, maximal aerobic speed or power, work and running economy, energy cost, and aerobic and anaerobic lactate thresholds. Seventeen systematic reviews were included in this umbrella review (12 with meta-analyses). Moderate to large effects were observed in all studies for running economy. Four meta-analyses examined the impact of strength training on V̇o2max, and none observed significant changes. Regarding endurance performance, 3 studies analyzed the impact of plyometric training and found small effects, except for 1 study, which found a large effect when compared with a control group. The risk-of-bias assessment revealed that most studies had low or critically low confidence levels, with issues in comprehensive literature searches, exclusion justifications, and handling publication bias. This umbrella review reveals that strength training improves endurance performance and running economy and helps maintain V̇o2max in middle- and long-distance endurance athletes. The review supports the general benefits of integrating strength training into endurance training programs.

records.title: Tissue Flossing: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Its Effects on Range of Motion, Pain, Muscle Strength, and Performance.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Tissue Flossing: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Its Effects on Range of Motion, Pain, Muscle Strength, and Performance.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Yao, L, Gan, J, Romagnoli, M, Liu, D, and Staiano, W. Tissue flossing: a systematic review and meta-analysis of its effects on range of motion, pain, muscle strength, and performance. J Strength Cond Res 40(2): 225-237, 2026-This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the acute effects of tissue flossing (TF) on joint range of motion (ROM), pain, muscle strength, and exercise performance in healthy individuals, also examining how subjects and intervention factors modify its efficacy. Databases (PubMed, Web of Science, EBSCO, Cochrane Library) were searched through September 2025 for randomized controlled and crossover trials involving TF in healthy subjects. Two independent reviewers handled screening, extraction, methodological quality assessment (Physiotherapy Evidence Database [PEDro] scale), and evidence grading (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation). We conducted meta-analyses, meta-regressions, and subgroup analyses by gender, training status, application site, and band pressure. Twenty studies ( n = 480) were included. Tissue flossing produced a trivial but significant ROM increase (Hedges' g = 0.19; 95% CI 0.05-0.33; p = 0.01). No significant effects appeared for muscle strength, muscle function, pain, sprint, or jump outcomes. Effectiveness varied by individual and intervention characteristics. The quality of evidence was moderate. Tissue flossing may acutely enhance joint ROM but does not significantly affect performance, and its benefits depend on individual and protocol variables. However, these conclusions are limited by the moderate quality of the available evidence, underscoring the need for more rigorous studies.

records.title: Comparative Efficacy of Various Exercise Types on Psychophysiological Outcomes in Colorectal Cancer Survivors: A Network Meta-Analysis.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Comparative Efficacy of Various Exercise Types on Psychophysiological Outcomes in Colorectal Cancer Survivors: A Network Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Purpose

This network meta-analysis aimed to evaluate and rank the comparative efficacy of aerobic training (AT), resistance training (RT), combined AT and RT (CT), and high-intensity interval training (HIIT) primarily on body weight and secondarily on body mass index (BMI), fat-free mass, fasting glucose, fasting insulin, handgrip strength, physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness, fatigue, quality of life, anxiety, depression, and exercise adherence in colorectal cancer (CRC) survivors.

Methods

MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CENTRAL, and MedRxiv were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) from inception up to July 1, 2025. RCTs published in English comparing exercise to controls (CON) or to another exercise type in CRC patients after colon resection surgery were qualified.

Results

Thirty-two studies involving 2001 CRC survivors (51.3/48.7 male-female ratio; mean ± standard deviation: age, 58.0 ± 10.2 years; BMI, 27.1 ± 3.9 kg·m -2 ) were included. HIIT and CT were more effective than CON in improving cardiorespiratory fitness and fasting insulin, respectively. No exercise type was identified as being more efficacious than CON in improving any other outcome measures. Nevertheless, HIIT had the highest probability of being the best exercise intervention for improving body weight, physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness, and quality of life. AT had the highest likelihood of reducing BMI, fasting glucose, and anxiety. CT had the highest probability of improving fasting insulin, fatigue, depression, and exercise adherence, while RT showed the highest probability of being the most effective exercise type in increasing handgrip strength and fat-free mass.

Conclusions

The current evidence indicates few confirmed benefits of exercise in CRC survivors, suggesting which types of exercise are most promising for a given psychophysiological outcome and may inform further large-scale RCTs of high methodological quality.

records.title: The Acute and Chronic Effects of Superset Resistance Training Versus Traditional Resistance Training-A Narrative Review.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: The Acute and Chronic Effects of Superset Resistance Training Versus Traditional Resistance Training-A Narrative Review.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Mang, ZA, Beam, JR, and Kravitz, L. The acute and chronic effects of superset resistance training versus traditional resistance training-A narrative review. J Strength Cond Res 39(11): 1216-1234, 2025-Resistance training (RT) leads to several health and performance benefits for a variety of people, including ball-sport athletes, occupational athletes, general population lifters, and elderly adults. Despite these well-established effects, a surprisingly high percentage of adults do not participate in consistent RT (∼80%), and several cite "perceived lack of time" as their primary barrier to RT. Superset training, which involves performing 2 or more consecutive sets of different exercises separated by short rest intervals, presents a time-efficient RT modality that reduces session duration by ∼50% compared with traditional RT (TRAD). Several applications of superset training exist, but this review focuses exclusively on the acute and chronic effects of agonist-antagonist paired sets (AAPS), reciprocal supersets (RSS), and total-body supersets (TBSS). The literature is particularly heterogeneous in its definitions, dependent variables, methodologies, and results, but acute data have generally demonstrated that muscle activation and training volume do not differ between supersets and TRAD. By contrast, power production is typically greater during TRAD, while training density, hormonal responses, blood lactate, energy expenditure, heart rate, oxygen consumption, and perceived exertion are greater during supersets. Exceptions exist, but chronic data generally indicate that supersets and TRAD lead to similar adaptations for endurance, hypertrophy, power, and strength. Considering the superior training density of AAPS, RSS, and TBSS, we tentatively conclude that superset programs deliver similar adaptations as TRAD in a more time-efficient manner.

records.title: Effect of exercise snacks on fitness and cardiometabolic health in physically inactive individuals: systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Effect of exercise snacks on fitness and cardiometabolic health in physically inactive individuals: systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objectives

To evaluate the effects of brief bouts of exercise spread throughout the day, termed 'exercise snacks', on cardiorespiratory and muscular fitness, and cardiometabolic health outcomes in physically inactive adults and older adults (aged ≥65 years).

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis.

Data sources

Seven databases were searched from inception to April 2025.

Eligibility criteria

Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of adults and older adults, comparing exercise snacks with non-exercising controls.

Results

11 RCTs (n=414; 69.1% women, mean age 18.7±0.8 to 74.2±5.6 years) were included. Exercise snacks were defined as structured bouts lasting ≤5 min, performed at least twice daily, ≥3 times/week, for ≥2 weeks. The interventions varied in duration (4-12 weeks), frequency (3-7 days/week) and intensity (moderate-to-vigorous to near-maximal). Exercise snacks significantly improved cardiorespiratory fitness in adults (g=1.37, 95% CI 0.58 to 2.17; p<0.005; I2=71.4 %, k=6) and muscular endurance in older adults (g=0.40, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.75; p=0.02; I2=0 %, k=4), with moderate and very low certainty of evidence, respectively. No significant effects were observed for lower limb muscular strength or cardiometabolic outcomes, including body composition, blood pressure and blood lipid profiles. High compliance (91.1%) and adherence (82.8%) rates were observed.

Conclusions

Moderate certainty of evidence indicated that exercise snacks improved cardiorespiratory fitness in physically inactive adults. However, evidence for benefits on muscular endurance in older adults was limited, and the current data do not support their effectiveness for improving other cardiometabolic health markers.

Prospero registration number

CRD42024616514.

records.title: Effects of muscle strength training combined with aerobic training versus aerobic training alone on cardiovascular disease risk indicators in patients with coronary artery disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials.

content.title: Effects of muscle strength training combined with aerobic training versus aerobic training alone on cardiovascular disease risk indicators in patients with coronary artery disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials.
content.abstract:
Objective

To compare the effects of aerobic training combined with muscle strength training (hereafter referred to as combined training) to aerobic training alone on cardiovascular disease risk indicators in patients with coronary artery disease (CAD).

Design

Systematic review with meta-analysis.

Data sources

MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, trial registries and grey literature sources were searched in February 2024.

Eligibility criteria

Randomised clinical trials comparing the effects of ≥4 weeks of combined training and aerobic training alone on at least one of the following outcomes: cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF), anthropometric and haemodynamic measures and cardiometabolic blood biomarkers in patients with CAD.

Results

Of 13 246 studies screened, 23 were included (N=916). Combined training was more effective in increasing CRF (standard mean difference (SMD) 0.26, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.49, p=0.03) and lean body mass (mean difference (MD) 0.78 kg, 95% CI 0.39 kg to 1.17 kg, p<0.001), and reducing per cent body fat (MD -2.2%, 95% CI -3.5% to -0.9%, p=0.001) compared with aerobic training alone. There were no differences in the cardiometabolic biomarkers between the groups. Our subgroup analyses showed that combined training increases CRF more than aerobic training alone when muscle strength training was added to aerobic training without compromising aerobic training volume (SMD 0.36, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.68, p=0.02).

Conclusion

Combined training had greater effects on CRF and body composition than aerobic training alone in patients with CAD. To promote an increase in CRF in patients with CAD, muscle strength training should be added to aerobic training without reducing aerobic exercise volume.

records.title: Impact of resistance training on cardiometabolic health-related indices in patients with type 2 diabetes and overweight/obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.

content.title: Impact of resistance training on cardiometabolic health-related indices in patients with type 2 diabetes and overweight/obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Objective

To evaluate the effects of resistance training on cardiometabolic health-related outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and overweight/obesity.

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs).

Data sources

PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Science Direct, Cochrane Library and Google Scholar databases were searched from inception up to May 2024. The search strategy included the following keywords: diabetes, resistance exercise and strength training.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

RCTs published in English comparing resistance training alone with non-exercising standard treatment. Participants were adults diagnosed with T2DM and concurrent overweight/obesity (body mass index (BMI) ≥25 kg/m2).

Results

A total of 18 RCTs qualified involving 1180 patients (48.6/51.4 female/male ratio; 63.3±7.0 years; 29.3±4.3 kg/m2). Waist circumference (standardised mean differences (SMD) -0.85 cm, 95% CI -1.66 to -0.04), waist-to-hip ratio (SMD -0.72, 95% CI -1.30 to -0.15), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (SMD +0.40 mg/dL, 95% CI 0.07 to -0.72), triglycerides (SMD -0.54 mg/dL, 95% CI -1.06 to -0.02), fasting blood glucose (SMD -0.65 mmol/L, 95% CI -1.19 to -0.12), fasting insulin (SMD -0.74 uIU/mL, 95% CI -1.12 to -0.36) and glycated haemoglobin (SMD -0.32%, 95% CI -0.63 to -0.01) improved compared with standard treatment. The risk of bias was low to unclear, and the quality of evidence was very low to moderate.

Conclusions

Resistance training as a standalone exercise intervention in the management and treatment of T2DM with concurrent overweight/obesity is associated with many cardiometabolic benefits when compared with standard treatment without exercise.

Prospero registration number

CRD42022355612.

records.title: Grading the evidence on the effects of exercise interventions in children and adolescents during and beyond cancer treatment: an umbrella review of systematic reviews with meta-analyses.

content.title: Grading the evidence on the effects of exercise interventions in children and adolescents during and beyond cancer treatment: an umbrella review of systematic reviews with meta-analyses.
content.abstract:
Objective

To synthesise the evidence on the effects of exercise interventions in children and adolescents during and beyond cancer treatment, and to evaluate the methodological quality and certainty of this evidence.

Design

Umbrella review of systematic reviews with meta-analyses.

Data source

PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and CINAHL were searched from inception to January 2026.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Systematic reviews with meta-analysis of controlled trials (randomised or non-randomised) evaluating exercise interventions in children and adolescents (≤19 years) during and beyond cancer treatment. Reviews without quantitative synthesis, those including only observational studies, or interventions where the isolated effect of exercise could not be determined were excluded.

Results

19 systematic reviews with meta-analyses, including 53 primary studies (n=2361 participants), were identified, yielding 80 effect estimates. Attending to the most comprehensive meta-analyses, exercise induced significant benefits on cardiorespiratory fitness (mean difference (MD) 6.92% (95% CI 1.01% to 12.82%)), cognitive function (standardised mean difference (SMD) 0.26 (95% CI 0.08 to 0.44)) and cognitive performance (SMD 0.41 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.65)), with moderate certainty of evidence. Exercise also induced significant benefits on muscle strength (SMD 0.81 (95% CI 0.05 to 1.57)), functional mobility (MD -1.17 s (95% CI -1.86 to -0.49)) and cancer-related fatigue (SMD -0.62 (95% CI -1.21 to -0.03)), although the certainty was low or very low. These effects were observed across meta-analyses focused exclusively on studies conducted during treatment (n=26), after treatment (n=3) or both (n=51). In contrast, no significant effects of exercise were observed for depression, bone mineral density, health-related quality of life, anthropometry or other clinical outcomes (such as mortality, relapse risk and withdrawal rates).

Conclusion

Exercise appears to be a beneficial intervention in childhood cancer for improving some physical, cognitive and psychosocial outcomes. However, more high-quality research is warranted to strengthen clinical recommendations and inform personalised exercise prescriptions, given that the certainty of evidence remains variable and overall low across outcomes.

Prospero registration number

CRD420251031412.

records.title: Clinical importance of simple muscular fitness tests to predict long-term health conditions: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 94 cohort studies.

content.title: Clinical importance of simple muscular fitness tests to predict long-term health conditions: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 94 cohort studies.
content.abstract:
Objective

To examine the predictive validity of field-based muscular strength tests in relation to incident long-term health conditions among adults.

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis.

Data sources

PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, CINAHL, Epistemonikos and Google Scholar.

Eligibility criteria

Cohort studies examining the predictive value of validated and/or reliable field-based muscular strength tests in relation to long-term health conditions in adults aged ≥18 years.

Results

A total of 155 studies were included with 94 included in the meta-analysis. Adults with the highest (vs lowest) handgrip strength levels had a lower risk of multiple long-term health conditions (all p<0.05), including cardiovascular diseases (OR=0.73; 95% CI 0.67 to 0.80), type 2 diabetes mellitus (OR=0.79; 95% CI 0.68 to 0.91), musculoskeletal impairment (OR=0.65; 95% CI 0.56 to 0.76), disability (OR=0.57; 95% CI 0.47 to 0.70), anxiety (OR=0.79; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.99), depression (OR=0.70; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.78), cognitive decline (OR=0.57; 95% CI 0.44 to 0.75), dementia (OR=0.62; 95% CI 0.53 to 0.73) and Parkinson's disease (OR=0.53; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.91). A 5 kg increase in handgrip strength was associated with a lower risk of developing most of these long-term health conditions. In turn, adults with the best (vs worst) performance on the 5-repetition chair-stand test had a lower risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus (OR=0.80; 95% CI 0.72 to 0.88), musculoskeletal impairment (OR=0.52; 95% CI 0.37 to 0.74), disability (OR=0.58; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.82), depression (OR=0.63; 95% CI 0.42 to 0.95), and dementia (OR=0.68; 95% CI 0.54 to 0.85). Every 1 s decrease was associated with 0.94 lower odds of musculoskeletal impairment. The overall quality of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate, indicating limited to moderate confidence in the results.

Conclusions

Our findings suggest increased handgrip strength and chair-stand test performance are associated with a lower risk of multiple long-term health conditions among adults. This research underscores the predictive value of simple field-based muscular strength tests which appear to be clinically useful for adults across different age groups and demographic profiles.

records.title: Efficacy of exercise interventions on prevention of sport-related concussion and related outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Efficacy of exercise interventions on prevention of sport-related concussion and related outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

To review the efficacy of exercise interventions on sport-related concussion (SRC) incidence, as well as on linear and rotational head accelerations, and isometric neck strength and to assess reporting completeness of exercise interventions using the Consensus on Exercise Reporting Template (CERT).

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis, according to the Prisma in Exercise, Rehabilitation, Sport medicine and SporTs science guidelines.

Data sources

Six databases (MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science CC and SPORTDiscus) were searched up to 26 June 2023.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Randomised controlled trials (RCTs), cluster RCTs or quasi-experimental studies, evaluating exercise interventions on SRC incidence, linear and rotational head accelerations, and/or isometric neck strength in male and/or female athletes of any age, and/or in a healthy general population.

Results

A total of 26 articles were included. A large effect size was observed for resistance training (RT) on isometric neck strength (standardised mean difference (SMD) 0.85; 95% CI 0.57 to 1.13; high-quality evidence). Non-significant effect sizes were observed for neuromuscular warm-up programmes on SRC incidence (risk ratio 0.69; 95% CI 0.39 to 1.23; low-quality evidence), or for RT on linear head acceleration (SMD -0.43; 95% CI -1.26 to 0.40; very low-quality evidence) or rotational head acceleration (SMD 0.08; 95% CI -0.61 to 0.77; low-quality evidence). No studies assessed the impact of RT on SRC incidence. CERT scores ranged from 4 to 16 (out of 19) with median score of 11.5 (IQR 9-13).

Conclusion

RT increases isometric neck strength, but the effect on SRC incidence is unknown. More adequately powered and rigorous trials are needed to evaluate the effect of exercise interventions on SRC incidence, and on linear and rotational head accelerations. Future studies should follow CERT guidelines, as the included interventions were generally not reported in sufficient detail for accurate replication.

Prospero registration number

CRD42023435033.

records.title: Effects of caffeine ingestion on endurance performance in acute hypoxic conditions: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of caffeine ingestion on endurance performance in acute hypoxic conditions: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract: Caffeine is a well-established aid for endurance performance under normoxic conditions. More recently, its ergogenic potential to improve endurance performance in hypoxia has attracted increasing interest, although findings remain inconsistent. This meta-analysis therefore evaluated the effects of caffeine on endurance performance under hypoxic conditions. PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched up to December 2025 for placebo-controlled, randomized crossover studies examining the impact of caffeine on endurance performance (e.g. time-trial and time-to-exhaustion) and physiological and/or metabolic responses (e.g. blood lactate concentration, heart rate, arterial oxygen saturation, and minute ventilation) in hypoxic conditions. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Meta-analyses were conducted in R software, comparing caffeine with placebo, with pooled effects calculated as Hedge's g using random-effects models. Nine studies were included (n = 117; female: n = 19). Caffeine significantly improved exercise performance in hypoxia, increasing exercise capacity across both time-to-exhaustion and time-trial tests (g = 0.76, 95% CI = 0.34 to 1.18, p < 0.001, low GRADE). Caffeine also increased heart rate, blood lactate concentration, and minute ventilation (g = 0.40 to 0.47, all p = 0.005, low GRADE). No significant effects were observed for ratings of perceived exertion or arterial oxygen saturation (g = -0.25 to 0.17, all p > 0.05, very low to low GRADE) under hypoxic conditions. This meta-analysis indicates that caffeine enhances endurance performance in hypoxic conditions and is accompanied by changes in key physiological and metabolic responses. Consequently, caffeine supplementation may serve as a practical strategy for attenuating hypoxia-induced performance impairments in athletes training or competing at altitude. Future high-quality, rigorously designed studies are warranted to further validate these effects.

records.title: Human Multi-Omics Meta-Analysis Identifies Molecular Layer-Specific Responses to Resistance and Endurance Exercise.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Human Multi-Omics Meta-Analysis Identifies Molecular Layer-Specific Responses to Resistance and Endurance Exercise.
content.abstract:
Purpose

Resistance and endurance exercise produce distinct adaptations, but molecular responses that distinguish these exercise modalities across studies and molecular layers remain incompletely defined. We sought to identify reproducible resistance- and endurance-associated molecular responses across human skeletal muscle and plasma omics datasets.

Methods

We integrated publicly available human exercise omics datasets. Random-effects meta-analyses included 15,312 genes from three skeletal muscle RNA-seq datasets and 4,641 proteins from two skeletal muscle proteomic datasets. Early skeletal muscle phosphoproteomic responses were compared across two independent studies using 2,430 matched phosphosites. At 24 hours, skeletal muscle phosphoproteomics and targeted and untargeted metabolomics in skeletal muscle and plasma were analyzed separately; plasma proteomics was not analyzed. Effects were standardized as resistance exercise minus endurance exercise, with significance defined within each molecular layer at FDR<0.05.

Results

RNA-seq identified 269 genes, including 71 resistance-associated and 198 endurance-associated genes. Global proteomics identified 10 proteins (nine resistance-associated; one endurance-associated). Early phosphoproteomic effects correlated across studies (r=0.589, P=4.1x10-227); 210 of 238 significant phosphosites were directionally concordant, and 51 met replication criteria. At 24 hours, targeted plasma metabolomics identified 14 endurance-associated features, while untargeted plasma metabolomics identified 18 features, including nine resistance-associated and nine endurance-associated features. Resistance-associated responses involved contractile, myofibrillar, cytoskeletal, extracellular matrix, protein quality-control, stress-response, and phosphorylation-related processes. Endurance-associated responses involved mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, respiratory-chain biology, fatty acid oxidation, substrate utilization, amino acid metabolism, and mitochondrial proteostasis.

Conclusions

Human molecular responses to resistance and endurance exercise are molecular-layer specific. Endurance-associated responses were more consistently represented in transcriptomic and metabolic layers, whereas resistance-associated responses were more prominent in protein abundance and phosphorylation. These findings provide a quantitative basis for selecting molecular measurements and sampling strategies in future human resistance and endurance exercise studies.

records.title: Large-Scale Evaluation of Performance and Biological Maturation in Post-PHV Youth Soccer Players: Sprinting, Jumping, Aerobic Fitness, and Functional Movement.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Large-Scale Evaluation of Performance and Biological Maturation in Post-PHV Youth Soccer Players: Sprinting, Jumping, Aerobic Fitness, and Functional Movement.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Akbaş, A, Hadyk, V, Bryk, P, Mazzei, S, Stanula, A, and Juras, G. Large-scale evaluation of performance and biological maturation in post-PHV youth soccer players: Sprinting, jumping, aerobic fitness, and functional movement. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study aimed to provide an integrated developmental profile of adolescent soccer players by examining how chronological age, biological maturation, and functional movement quality interact to shape sprint, jump, and aerobic fitness performance. A total of 246 male athletes (U15-U17) from 5 elite youth soccer academies completed sprint, jump, change-of-direction (COD), and aerobic tests alongside Functional Movement Screen (FMS) and Y-Balance Test (YBT) assessments. Maturity offset (years from peak height velocity, PHV) was used to estimate biological age, and group differences were analyzed using analysis of variance and analysis of covariance, with statistical significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements with age were observed in sprinting, jumping, and aerobic fitness (p < 0.001); however, after controlling for PHV, differences in jumping and COD performance were no longer significant, whereas sprint performance and aerobic fitness remained age-dependent. Functional movement and balance showed small age-related differences that were largely explained by maturational variation. Weak and inconsistent correlations between FMS, YBT, and performance (|r| ≈ 0.20-0.35) suggested partial independence between movement quality and motor output. Notably, in older players, higher scores in mobility-related FMS components were associated with slower sprinting, a pattern that may reflect-rather than cause-reduced mechanical efficiency associated with greater flexibility. These findings indicate that post-PHV players are not a homogeneous group and support the use of maturity-informed, multidimensional athlete monitoring to guide individualized training even after PHV.

records.title: Does Increased Maximal Sprint Speed Alter Pacing Distribution in the 400-m Race Among Male 400-m Sprinters? A Longitudinal Study.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Does Increased Maximal Sprint Speed Alter Pacing Distribution in the 400-m Race Among Male 400-m Sprinters? A Longitudinal Study.
content.abstract: Sato, K, Yoshimoto, T, Chiba, Y, Ohnuma, H, Iso, S, Tsuchiya, J, and Takai, Y. Does increased maximal sprint speed alter pacing distribution in the 400-m race among male 400-m sprinters? A longitudinal study. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Performance in the 400-m sprint is influenced not only by short sprint ability but also by pacing strategy during a race. However, the effects of changes in short sprint ability on pacing characteristics remain unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to clarify the effects of changes in maximal sprint speed (MSS) on 400-m sprint performance and segmental running speed in competitive 400-m sprinters. Twenty-three male 400-m sprinters (age: 20.04 ± 1.76 years, height: 1.75 ± 0.06 m, body mass: 66.93 ± 6.93 kg, 400-m personal best: 49.03 ± 1.56 seconds; range: 45.58-52.70 seconds) performed 400-m and 60-m sprint tests on 2 occasions separated by 1 year. Maximal sprint speed was defined as the highest mean running speed among the 10-m segments during a 60-m sprint. In the 400-m sprint, the relative running speed for each 50-m segment (%MSS) was calculated as the mean running speed divided by the MSS, and the percentage of the 400-m time spent in each 50-m segment (%ST) was determined. Sprinters who exhibited greater increases in MSS demonstrated greater improvements in 400-m sprint performance. Furthermore, increases in MSS were significantly associated with improvements in running speed during the 0-250-m segments of the 400-m sprint. These findings indicate that increases in MSS may contribute to improvements in 400-m sprint performance, particularly through enhanced running speed during the first half of the race.

records.title: The Respiratory Compensation Point Predicts 19.2-km Cycling Performance in Trained Male Cyclists.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: The Respiratory Compensation Point Predicts 19.2-km Cycling Performance in Trained Male Cyclists.
content.abstract:
Abstract

So, YLI, Faricier, R, Guluzade, NA, Belfry, GR, Murias, JM, and Keir, DA. The respiratory compensation point predicts 19.2-km cycling performance in trained male cyclists. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study tested the hypothesis that the step-ramp-step (SRS)-corrected cycling power output (PO) at the respiratory compensation point (RCP) predicts cycling time-trial performance and explored the independent and collective contributions to trial time of 4 physiological variables derived from single or repeated SRS protocols: peak oxygen uptake (V̇o2peak), cycling economy, RCP, and fatigue resistance. Twenty-eight trained male cyclists completed an SRS protocol before and after a 19.2-km virtual time trial (∼30 minutes) on their personal road bikes using a smart trainer. V̇o2peak, cycling economy, and SRS-corrected PO at RCP were derived from the pre-time-trial SRS protocol. Fatigue resistance was quantified as the change in peak ramp PO from pre- to post-time trial. Independent and multilinear regression evaluated the predictive strength of each variable. Relative SRS-corrected RCP (W·kg-1) showed the strongest independent correlation with time-trial completion time (r = -0.61, p < 0.001). Relative V̇o2peak (mL·kg-1·min-1) and cycling economy (%) were also moderately associated with time-trial performance (r = -0.42, p = 0.03; and r = -0.55, p < 0.001, respectively), whereas fatigue resistance was not significantly correlated. In the multilinear regression analysis, SRS-corrected RCP uniquely explained 30.9% of the model's total predictive variance (r = 0.68, p < 0.01) followed by cycling economy (21.3%), ΔPOpeak (2.1%), and absolute V̇o2peak (3.3%). Among trained male cyclists, relative PO at SRS-corrected RCP is a strong and independent predictor of ∼30-minute time-trial performance. The SRS protocol provides a practical, single-session method to assess key physiological determinants of endurance performance, with valuable applications for training prescription and athlete monitoring.

records.title: Sex-specific Lower Limb Strength, Flexibility, and Running Biomechanics in Adolescents With and Without Osgood-Schlatter Disease.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Sex-specific Lower Limb Strength, Flexibility, and Running Biomechanics in Adolescents With and Without Osgood-Schlatter Disease.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To examine sex-specific lower limb strength, flexibility, and running biomechanics in adolescents with and without OSD.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective chart review of 100 adolescents (n=25 each group): females with OSD (age=14.6 ± 1.9 y; body mass index [BMI]=21.3 ± 2.1 kg/m2); males with OSD (age=14.4 ± 1.6 y; BMI=21.7 ± 3.2 kg/m2); females without OSD (age=14.8 ± 2.2 y; BMI=21.7 ± 3.0 kg/m2); and males without OSD (age=14.4 ± 2.2 y; BMI=22.0 ± 4.6 kg/m2). We assessed mass-normalized sagittal and frontal hip strength and sagittal knee strength via hand-held dynamometry, and quadriceps femoris (prone knee flexion) and hip flexor (Thomas test) flexibility. Limb crossover, contralateral pelvic drop [CPD], medial knee displacement, and tibial dominant stride were assessed during treadmill running. Group differences were analyzed using a two-way multivariate analysis of variance (continuous outcomes) and logistic regression (categorical outcomes), covarying for age and BMI. Analyses were performed using SPSS (alpha set at p<0.05).

Results

Compared with sex-matched healthy peers, females with OSD had impaired hip abduction strength and a greater propensity for CPD and medial knee displacement, though greater hip flexion strength (p≤0.03; Table). Males with OSD had greater hip and knee sagittal plane strength yet impaired flexibility (p≤0.02; Table). Compared with males with OSD, females with OSD had lower hip and knee strength, greater quadriceps femoris flexibility, and higher odds of frontal plane biomechanical deficits (p≤0.02; Table).

Conclusion

We observed sex-specific differences in lower limb muscular and biomechanical features in adolescents with OSD, suggesting that clinicians should consider sex-specific rehabilitation strategies for adolescents with OSD.

records.title: Should They Start or Not? A Comparative Analysis of Starter and Nonstarter Preseason Fitness Characteristics in NCAA Division III Baseball.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Should They Start or Not? A Comparative Analysis of Starter and Nonstarter Preseason Fitness Characteristics in NCAA Division III Baseball.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Schilling, DT, Abraham, TR, and Elazzazi, A. Should they start or not? A comparative analysis of starter and nonstarter preseason fitness characteristics in NCAA Division III baseball. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Preseason fitness testing in baseball is a widely adopted practice to assess the physical preparedness of players. However, the relationship between these preseason fitness assessments, their ability to differentiate starters from nonstarters in the subsequent season, and their relationship to preseason coaching evaluations is not well-established. This exploratory study aimed to provide a preseason profile of men's NCAA Division III baseball players, compare the differences between starting and nonstarting players, and explore the relationship of these preseason measures to the offensive performance of the starting players at the completion of the season. Starters were considered any hitter who averaged at least 2 plate appearances per team game played or participated in at least 75% of the team's games. Twenty-six players performed 8 preseason fitness tests; and the head coach, blinded to all preseason fitness testing results, subjectively rated the players' batting (power, ball contact, and form) and running performance (speed, agility, and form), resulting in a total offensive performance score (TOPS). In-season offensive performance was measured by each player's on-base plus slugging percentage (OPS). Starters demonstrated significantly greater batted ball velocity, countermovement vertical jump height, unilateral lateral to medial jump distance, medicine ball throw velocity, and faster 60-yard dash and agility T-test times relative to nonstarters. Notably, no significant correlations were observed between any physical performance variable and OPS or TOPS, suggesting that preseason fitness testing may reflect athletic readiness but does not directly relate to offensive performance or coaching evaluation outcomes in this sample.

records.title: Hematological and biochemical responses to three doses of caffeine during the CrossFit® workout: a randomized, double-blind, crossover trial.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Hematological and biochemical responses to three doses of caffeine during the CrossFit® workout: a randomized, double-blind, crossover trial.
content.abstract:
Background

This study investigated the effects of three doses of caffeine (CAF) on hematological and biochemical responses during the CrossFit® workout, a protocol known to induce significant physiological fluctuations.

Methods

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo (PLA)-controlled crossover trial, 26 moderately trained CrossFit® athletes received acute doses of 3, 6, or 9 mgCAF/kgbody mass (BM), or a PLA, 70 min before a 17-min CrossFit® workout.

Results

While exercise was the predominant driver of hematological changes, with no CAF-specific modulation of blood cell indices, significant treatment × time point interactions were observed solely for glucose concentration. Specifically, MEDIUM (6 mgCAF/kgBM) and HIGH (9 mgCAF/kgBM) CAF doses produced significantly greater post-exercise glucose elevations compared to baseline and PLA visits. Phosphates concentrations increased over time, particularly post-exercise, with no treatment effect retained after excluding baseline visit in the sensitivity analysis. Calcium level dynamics were influenced by temporal factors rather than CAF, and magnesium concentration remained stable.

Conclusions

These findings suggest that acute CAF ingestion selectively influences post-exercise glucose responses during the CrossFit® workout, whereas hematological variables and most biochemical markers remain unaffected. Significant post-exercise glucose elevations were observed following the 6 and 9 mgCAF/kgBM conditions compared with baseline and PLA visits, while serum mineral concentrations remained largely stable across treatments.

Clinical trials registration

NCT03822663.

records.title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To investigate the effects of caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 and 6 mg/kg on reactive blocking timing, block-jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses in elite female volleyball players under post-fatigue conditions.

Methods

Fifteen elite female volleyball players completed a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study implemented with double-blinding procedures. Participants consumed placebo (PLA), caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 mg/kg (CAF3) or 6 mg/kg (CAF6), and were tested after supplementation and warm-up at PRE and immediately after a volleyball-specific repeated blocking fatigue protocol (POST). Primary outcomes were reactive blocking timing-chain indices and block-jump (BJ) peak power. Secondary outcomes included additional BJ mechanical variables and general jump measures from countermovement jump (CMJ) and drop jump (DJ) tests. Exploratory outcomes included synchronized surface electromyography (sEMG) variables of lower-limb muscles. Participant blinding was assessed after each visit.

Results

Fatigue impaired jump-related performance across conditions (p < 0.05). For the primary outcomes, the descriptive decline in BJ peak power was 6.9% in CAF6 versus 13.9% in PLA; the adjusted POST comparison did not establish superiority of CAF6 over CAF3. For timing outcomes, overall sequence time increased by 18.4% in PLA, 6.4% in CAF3, and 3.0% in CAF6; CAF6 therefore showed the smallest descriptive deterioration in the integrated sequence measure, whereas CAF3 showed little change in the mean stationary and movement component times. CAF6 showed a reduction in mean stationary response time and the smallest increase in overall sequence time. For secondary outcomes, caffeine showed more favorable post-fatigue responses in selected CMJ/DJ measures, including CMJ mean propulsive power and DJ contact time (p < 0.05), and CAF6 showed greater preservation of selected stretch-shortening cycle-related mechanical measures, including DJ jump height and DJ vertical stiffness, than PLA (p < 0.05). In contrast, CMJ mRSI showed a divergent pattern and was not interpreted as evidence of caffeine-related attenuation of fatigue-induced decrements. Exploratory sEMG results showed smaller post-fatigue changes in selected frequency-domain and activation-timing variables under CAF6, particularly in measures related to extensor-muscle function. Participant masking was incomplete: perceived caffeine ingestion was reported in 0.0%, 53.3%, and 80.0% of PLA, CAF3, and CAF6 visits, respectively, and adverse effects were more frequent in CAF6.

Conclusions

The observed responses were outcome-specific: CAF6 showed a smaller decline in BJ peak power and the smallest increase in overall sequence time, whereas CAF3 showed little change in mean stationary and movement response times. These findings do not establish a generally preferable dose or a timing-stability advantage for CAF3. Incomplete participant masking limits attribution of the differences exclusively to caffeine dose.

records.title: Novel creatine formulation exhibits similar serum creatine concentrations and pharmacokinetics to creatine monohydrate in healthy adults.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Novel creatine formulation exhibits similar serum creatine concentrations and pharmacokinetics to creatine monohydrate in healthy adults.
content.abstract:
Background

Creatine monohydrate (CrM) is the most widely studied creatine form, demonstrating robust efficacy, bioavailability, and safety. With creatine growing in popularity, alternative formulations of creatine have been developed to target solubility and to optimize absorption pharmacokinetics (PK), as well as to reduce gastrointestinal (GI) intolerability. The purpose of the current study was to evaluate the acute effects of a novel creatine monohydrate (OptiCreatineTM; CrO) compared to CrM on serum creatine PK and GI tolerability in healthy adults.

Methods

Healthy, recreationally active adults (age: 22 ± 3 years; males n = 8, females n = 9) consumed a single 5-gram dose of CrM or CrO across two separate visits following an overnight fast, in a randomized, double-blind, crossover design. Venous blood samples were collected at baseline and 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, and 300 mins post-ingestion of their assigned treatment to assess serum creatine concentrations. PK parameters including peak concentration (Cmax), time to peak (Tmax), absorption rate constant (ka), elimination rate constant (kel; h-1), and area under the curve (AUC₀-T) were derived using nonlinear regression modeling. GI symptoms were assessed using validated questionnaires.

Results

There was no difference in serum creatine concentrations between CrM or CrO across all participants (p = 0.707), males (p = 0.318), or females (p = 0.996) at any time point. Serum creatine increased over time regardless of treatment (p < 0.0001). No differences were observed between CrM and CrO for Cmax (mean difference ± standard deviation (MD ± SD): 7.66 ± 50.37μM; p = 0.82), Tmax (MD ± SD: -0.04 ± 0.13 h; p = 0.54), ka (MD ± SD: -0.15 ± 0.45 h-1; p = 0.51), kel (MD ± SD: 0.01 ± 0.03 h-1; p = 0.61), or AUC₀-T (MD ± SD: 22.09 ± 160.57 μM·h; p = 0.74), with no sex × treatment interactions (p ≥ 0.05). Descriptive evaluation showed similar GI symptom profiles between conditions, with low frequency and minimal severity reported across both treatments.

Conclusions

A single 5-gram dose of CrO produced similar serum creatine and PK characteristics to CrM in healthy adults. These findings support CrO as a viable delivery option, with no significant differences in acute pharmacokinetic profiles or GI tolerability compared to CrM.

records.title: Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (aronia melanocarpa) supplementation modulates exercise-induced changes in iron metabolism in female swimmers.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (aronia melanocarpa) supplementation modulates exercise-induced changes in iron metabolism in female swimmers.
content.abstract:
Background

Intense exercise may transiently alter iron metabolism through inflammatory and oxidative mechanisms. Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa) may influence these responses and short-term iron regulation. This study evaluated the effects of black chokeberry supplementation on iron metabolism, inflammation, antioxidant capacity, and hematological status in female competitive swimmers.

Methods

Twenty-two female swimmers (13.14 ± 1.42 years) were randomly allocated to a supplementation or placebo group. Participants completed two identical swimming tests comprising 800-, 200-, and 50-m efforts before and after 57.32 ± 8.31 days of supplementation. Blood was collected before exercise, immediately after exercise, and after 3 h of recovery.

Results

Most inflammatory markers showed time-dependent changes without significant group effects. C-reactive protein decreased from pre- to post-exercise during the second test in the supplemented group (p = 0.0325; Cohen's d = 1.29), whereas placebo recovery values increased between tests (p < 0.0001; Cohen's d = 3.33). Total antioxidant capacity showed a significant time × group interaction (p = 0.0007), with higher recovery values in the supplemented group. Iron, unsaturated iron-binding capacity, and total iron-binding capacity showed significant time effects (all p < 0.0001). Hepcidin also showed a significant time effect, with significant within-group increases only in the placebo group. Transferrin was lower in the supplemented group at Post II (p = 0.0071; Cohen's d = 1.17), whereas ferritin remained unchanged and hematological parameters showed no consistent between-group differences.

Conclusion
